speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgency, a matter of deep concern. It relates to the announcement made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs to the effect that a 7.2 per cent increase in the rate of the war disability pension will come into effect in January. This increase, already provided by law, does not restore the basic rate to the composite level established in 1973, a level which the minister agreed was one which should be maintained. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and concerns the general area of economic sanctions and boycotts. Bearing in mind the economic and commercial sanctions against South Africa which were announced yesterday, could the Prime Minister explain the double standard when the Canadian Government feels it is quite moral and ethical to offer a $100 million loan to Cuba through EDC to finance a stainless steel mill when that country has troops in Angola and several other South African countries and supplies arms to guerrilla forces in Africa?

speechtext:
Not except in South Africa. Mr. Speaker, we are making no legislation to prevent Canadian businessmen trading in South Africa if they so desire. There is absolutely no restriction on the issuance of passports for them if they want to go and trade or play tennis or practice sports. It is the policy of this government that Canadians are free to move wherever they want, whenever they want. We do say that the federal government will not encourage or subsidize such movements in the case of South Africa. We went even further in the case of Rhodesia. Businessmen can move there if they want to, but we will not in any way permit or authorize the trade of goods with that country because under the United Nations Security Council resolution there is an embargo on trade with South Africa.
In the case of South Africa, Canada had an embargo on the sale of arms long before the Security Council adopted this resolution. We were away ahead of the United States and the Security Council on this matter but now this is also the policy of the Security Council that there should be no trade in arms with South Africa. There is therefore a certain limit on trade in arms with South Africa. The United Nations did not go that far in the case of Chile, in the case of Cuba, in the case of China, in the case of the Soviet Union, in the case of Czechoslovakia, in the case of Rumania or in the case of a devil of a lot of other countries who do not have democracy and who do not have ideologies in which we believe but in which case not only businessmen are free to trade and move there but in each case our government services, trade commissions and so on, are prepared to assist them in passage of this trade. We believe that as a general rule, trade between nations is a good thing. It is not only good economically but it is also good in terms of human relations between the peoples of these countries.

The House resumed from Monday, December 19, 1977, consideration of the motion of Mr. Jamieson that this House takes note of the present state and future prospects of Canada's relationships with other nations of the world.

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated last evening, most of my remarks on this interesting debate will be directed toward the coming United Nations conference on disarmament. Before commencing to deal with that particular subject, I want to respond to the proposal made by the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) yesterday in regard to South Africa. As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) indicated, we welcome that particular initiative. Actually, we consider it to be approximately ten years late.
We should like to look at the pig in the poke because we are not sure what it means. Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs will flesh out this proposal. The Secretary of State has suggested that Canada will develop a code of ethics for Canadian companies which deal with South Africa. That is all very well, but unless we know what are the sanctions to be applied to those who violate the code, to a large extent that statement is meaningless.
In regard to the response of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), I have concern about the statement he made as reported at page 2007 of Hansard dated December 19, 1977, which reads as follows:
As we study these implications-
Perhaps this statement is an indication of the Conservative policy. I hope it is not. When the Leader of the Opposition referred to "implications", he was referring to implications on the proposal of South Africa. Perhaps other participants in this debate may correct what appears to be a rather naive statement. It continues:
As we study these implications, one of those matters to which we will want to pay close attention is to ensure that their negative impact will not fall more particularly upon residents of that country who are black. We think that would be a most counterproductive approach to Canadian policy, as we are sure the minister will agree-
External Affairs
If any member of this House believes that we should not exercise sanctions against a country with a largely black population, on the ground that it will hurt the black population, he does not understand what the black populations of those countries want. If members consulted with the leaders of the black communities in South Africa, I am sure they would discover that these sanctions have not gone far enough. While there may be some short-term economic loss to blacks, those people welcome initiatives on the part of western industrial countries in order to move their country forward to a civilized and democratic system.
This House has heard a long debate regarding the question of which countries should be singled out for these particular sanctions. It is not a simple question, nor is it a simple issue. Moral decisions have to be taken. I suggest to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) that when South Africa is isolated as a special case, Chile also should be isolated as a special and separate case. As far as Chile is concerned, western industrial countries assisted in the subversion of the democratic elected government of that country. Surely, that places Chile in a special category. The moral arguments the government is making in regard to South Africa should apply to Chile, even though it is a different case. These judgments are made subjectively.
What about Cuba?

My hon. friend asks me about Cuba. If aid in the world is to be examined, we must examine who is receiving the aid and how much of it is being directed to people who need it. If you use that as your moral judgment, you will continue to have good relations with Cuba because Cuba is one country that has taken aid. No matter how much we may disagree with their regime, you will find that the aid which has gone to Cuba has in fact gone to people who need it. That should be the criterion all around the world. When we aid countries in Africa and Asia, we should make sure that aid is going to the poor and starving who need it, certainly not to monuments growing up to a totalitarian dictator, as has happened so often with aid. That is not what is happening in Cuba.
What about human rights?
What about a speech?

If the hon. member would like to rise to his feet and make a speech, he can do so. However, I do not mind responding on the question of human rights. As I said yesterday, we should stop being selective about human rights. We must remember that there are other countries beside the Soviet Union which mistreat their citizens. If there are people being tortured in Cuba, we should be on the floor of the House calling out their names, just as we do in any other regime around the world. So the idea that we keep throwing the names of countries back and forth at each other, on the

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
assumption that somehow this party is only interested in human rights in certain countries, or that party is only interested in human rights in certain other countries, is simply a non sequitur; it is simply irrelevant.
I should like to get back, however, to what has really happened to this country over the past ten years, particularly the image of this country in international affairs. I have had the opportunity to attend every Law of the Sea Conference since they began, and it is the general consensus around the world that this country's reputation as a peacemaker has suffered very seriously since the days when Lester Pearson was conducting the foreign affairs of this country.
There are a number of reasons for this, but one of the major ones has been our slavish acceptance of any policy in this world promoted by the United States state department. So long as this country continues to take a satellite position in world affairs, its reputation will continue to suffer. I should like to remind hon. members of some of the things this country has done in the past which has won it the reputation of being an aggressive peacemaker. They are: the Canadian refusal to support the U.S. boycott of Cuba; Canada's strong disapproval of the Anglo-French-Israel invasion of Egypt of 1956; the Prime Minister's visits to China and Russia; and the disapproval by this country of the massive bombing of Vietnam. These are all foreign policy matters in which Canada stood up and was independent on the side of peace, and it was because of those policies that we gained a reputation as peacemakers.
But our reputation today is no more that of a peacemaker. We have not engaged, in the international sphere, with the kind of aggressiveness, originality and initiative that our diplomats and our governments once had. Surely, at this time, we should have entered into these kinds of initiatives. Another initiative was taken by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), who I see here today, who established that kind of independence in foreign policy with the initiative he took at the Commonwealth conference to exclude South Africa from the Commonwealth.
Here, again, was a foreign policy initiative where Canada stood up and said something independently and differently. If there is anything this country needs, it is to have independence. It needs a sense of nationhood. It can have that sense of nationhood through such a foreign policy. But what has been the record for the last ten years? The record has been a slavish, following whatever policies happen to be adopted at the time in the United States.
So long as we see our role as merely that of a satellite or supporter of the United States, we are not doing ourselves credit and we are not contributing to our own relationships with the United States. Nor are we contributing to peace in the world, because the United States is entitled to have us as an objective friend and to have from us the kind of advice which may be different from the advice they have been receiving their own bureaucrats. That has not been the case. In the United Nations we have simply been slavishly following the United States example in one motion after another.
[Mr. Leggatt.l
In the province of British Columbia there is very real concern about the establishment of the Trident nuclear submarine base in Bangor, Washington, which is some 60 miles south of the city of Victoria. It is not an easy issue, but when I wrote to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the response may as well have come from the U.S. government-there would have been hardly any difference.
Let me just quote the response, to give a little background. There has been real concern among some scientists that this particular weapon was being developed as a first-strike weapon because of the technical facility that was available to target the nuclear warheads right on the sites of the silos of Soviet missile sites, thereby at least providing some temptation for a first-strike capacity. That issue was never addressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is the present government House leader. He said this in response to my letter:
The Trident submarine programme is being undertaken by the U.S.A. in the development of its strategic deterrent. Because the programme does not form part of the Canada-U.S. arrangements for the joint defence of North America and the proposed base at Bangor will be built on U.S. territory, there is no requirement for the U.S.A. to consult Canada with regard to this matter and we have not made any representations to the U.S. authorities on the subject.
Here is a matter which intimately affects the safety and future of people all over the world. Surely we could at least expect enough interest on the part of this government to determine at least what kind of weapon it wants on our doorstep and what effect that weapon will have on the mutually assured destruction theory which many people tell us has kept the peace. There is merely a slavish adoption of the U.S. foreign policy. Why is the UN disarmament conference so vital, not merely to this country but to the whole world?
In 1973, the world spent S240 billion on armaments. It went up from $160 million ten years previously. If we were to take 10 per cent of the saving on the world armament bill, here are some of the things we could do: we could eliminate all illiteracy in the world by the turn of the century, simply by spending $1.5 billion of that money. We could feed the hungry of the world at the rate of $4 billion a year, and there would be no more hungry children in the world.
We could provide a family planning program of some $2 billion a year which would once and for all begin to tackle the major problem in this world, which is overpopulation. We could provide a worldwide medical care scheme at the rate of $4 billion a year. We could treble our foreign aid at $3.5 billion, and we could provide a permanently funded peacekeeping force at $1.5 billion a year. That is by simply reducing the expenditure of the world, on armaments, by 10 per cent. It is growing at a faster rate than 10 per cent. By simply reducing it to 10 per cent, we would at last tackle some of the global problems.
How do we go about moving this question forward? How do we, as a country, go to the United Nations disarmament conference and do something in terms of stating that we have a commitment to the principle of disarmament? There is not
December 20, 1977

much point in going there talking out of both sides of our mouths, selling arms around the world and then suggesting that we cut back. There is not much point in saying we believe that action is needed to reduce the proliferation of nuclear weapons while selling the dangerous CANDU reactor around the world to every unstable regime that is willing to buy one with a set of safety standards which is becoming a laughingstock in terms of scientific research into the risks inherent in the CANDU reactor.
In my view, what we have to do is take some unilateral action. It takes courage to act alone in these matters, but we are in a rather unique position. We can make unilateral decisions which will not adversely affect us and which may move the world forward in terms of disarmament. There is ample precedent for this. There is a treaty which controls the use of bacteriological warfare. That treaty came about because of the actions of former President Nixon of the United States, who acted unilaterally in saying that the United States would end its continuing moves toward bacteriological warfare. When he acted unilaterally, the Soviet Union joined the United States, and there is a treaty. Canada also acted unilaterally in forgiving some $254 million of debts of the poorest countries of the world. That act of generosity spurred Sweden forward, and Sweden did exactly the same thing. That did not come about as a result of a continuing dialogue which took forever. There has to be a break in the log-jam.
I suggest that in three areas we can move this country forward in a very significant way and make a significant contribution to the world UN conference. Right now, Canada ranks sixth in the world in terms of sales of weaponry to other countries. Those sales amount to about $355 million a year. Over a ten-year period we sold about $78 million worth of hardware to Peru, $49 million to Brazil, and $45 million to Iran. My hon. friend was wondering about Cuba. We sold none to Cuba. We sold $25 million worth of weaponry to Malaysia and $1 million to Chile. Of course, that was subsequent to the change of regime in Chile. We are making a pretty hefty profit in arms sales around the world. Surely in order to move to a position of less hypocrisy on this subject at the UN conference we should make a unilateral declaration that we will suspend for one year, while the conference is on, our sales of arms abroad and invite other like-minded countries to join us.
The second, and perhaps the most important unilateral act we could take, would be to abandon our nuclear role in the world. I know that our nuclear role is very peripheral. We have some storage of nuclear weapons at two or three bases in Canada, but my information is that the abandonment of our nuclear role would not in any way affect the capacity of the United States in terms of the defence of the North American continent. To abandon that peripheral role would be an important step forward. More importantly, abandoning our sales of the CANDU nuclear reactor abroad is absolutely vital.
In the world there are two kinds of proliferation, horizontal proliferation between major countries, and vertical proliferation of atomic weaponry-the more dangerous. As surely as
External Affairs
we are sitting in this House, terrorist groups will get hold of a nuclear weapon. The Japanese Red Army received $6 million from the government of Japan not too long ago in a hijacking. As a world community, surely we must ask ourselves how we are to stop the inevitable from happening. We cannot stop it by wringing our hands. First, we have to study the way we are securing our airports. It is still most unsatisfactory. More importantly, we have to take a careful look at the way we are proliferating peaceful nuclear technology around the world and making more and more of the byproducts of the CANDU reactor available to terrorist groups.
The day a terrorist gets a nuclear bomb and blackmails a major city or country will be the day of Canada's shame, because that is the day Canada will have contributed to that act. The very real risk of war and the risk to the human race now is the risk of terrorism and the risk of terrorists obtaining a nuclear weapon.
We have abandoned the role of peacemaker because we have made compromises. We have gone ahead and sold nuclear materials regardless of the cost because of pride in our technology and the bureaucracy, the business and the labouring people who work in that industry. Altogether, it is a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. The ball is rolling. The momentum is there, and this government has never been strong enough to stop it. What we need is a government which has the guts to stand up to its bureaucracy and say, "No more sales of nuclear weaponry and nuclear technology abroad". The day we do that we will make a significant contribution to peace and to this particular conference.
Last, but not least, we have abandoned the question of peace research. War and peace are both subject to scientific study. The amount we spend in terms of contributions to war is massive. In terms of peace research, I suggest we give nothing. We should commit 10 per cent of our military budget to peace research and to approved peace study groups. Sweden has done this for many years. We no longer have that reputation. I want to mention one group, the Canadian Peace Research Institute, which has been struggling on a very small budget and with no help whatsoever from this government for a very long time. Surely we should be moving forward in terms of world peace.
I want to conclude on an optimistic note. Most disarmament conferences work only under pressure. I do not believe the United Nations itself would have been formed without the memory of the agony of the Second World War. So we have to ask ourselves what pressure is now on the delegates who will attend the conference. There is pressure because of nuclear weaponry and because of the very real risk that it will get into the hands of either a terrorist group or a small and unstable country.
Canada has done almost nothing-in fact, less than nothing-to prevent that weaponry from going to unstable parts of the world. I believe we could make a positive contribution if we were to, in a unilateral way, move the conference forward; but if we simply go with the same hypocritical attitude we have had for the past ten years, Canada will not only not be listened to but will not have any impact on the conference.

December 20, 1977
External Affairs

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed this debate with a great deal of interest. I have read everything that was said yesterday in my absence, and I have listened to the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) who always commands attention when he speaks in the House.
I welcome the opportunity to discuss international affairs. This has been a closed shop since the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. The day I asked the Deputy Prime Minister whether consideration would be given to setting aside a couple of days for discussion of external affairs, I knew in advance what his answer would be. He is one who through the years has dedicated himself to parliament. I often think he must feel lost sitting among those who today are in the same cabinet and who seem to regard parliament as an institution of little or no consequence, realizing in advance, as they do, that whatever stand they take, a supine majority will ensure passage of legislation regardless of whether it is for the benefit of Canada.
Over the years, under the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and under my government, whenever there was a request for a debate on external affairs it was granted. The present minister, too, shares the appreciation of the assistance which parliament can give to a government when members speak freely concerning matters with which they are conversant and of which they have knowledge.
There were times in the past when I represented Canada at various conferences both before and after I became prime minister. Since 1963, for some reason I have never had the opportunity of going to any conference even in a minor capacity. I can only conclude the reason is that I do not have those qualifications which other members of the House have.
On this occasion 1 will discuss a number of matters which I believe deserve to be considered. I am not surprised-I have become inured to it-that whenever I am about to speak, or am on any list to speak, the Prime Minister always finds that some other call takes him from the chamber. Were he here, I would be able to make some personal references because he chose to forget my Christian name today. I can understand any relationship to anything Christian he might find discomforting having regard to the degree to which he has so often in the past been able to secure his inspiration from non-religious sources. I regret, too, with the minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) the fact that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) is not here to speak. This House has, for him, that feeling of respect which comes to those who, regardless of whether one agrees with his political views or not, is recognized as one who is prepared to speak as he feels.
I must say that I am very much interested in what has been decided in connection with South Africa, to which I intend to make reference later. One thing that strikes me about this government, however, is the abiding affection that is shown to Castro and to Cuba. Whatever offence is committed in that country is covered up, concealed, approved or at least con-

nived. These are things that are difficult to understand. Canada does not want to be "Castronated".
Hear, hear!
Canada does not support any nation or national leader whose objective is civil war and launching it in other parts of the world.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear!
The minister says, "Hear, hear." I hope he will say "Hear, hear", when opportunities come to determine that Castro and his works are taboo in this country.
Hear, hear!

Castro has gone all over Africa launching civil wars. Castro has American republics deeply concerned over what he has been doing to undermine their governments in favour of communist governments or far left institutions. In Great Britain, in the United States, in Prance and in West Germany I have spoken to the leaders of those countries. They cannot understand the close and abiding relationship that prevails between the Prime Minister of Canada and Castro. An international brigand-that is what he is-who has his forces destroy freedom in African countries, is endeavouring to undermine democratic governments in Central and South America. Yet he is Canada's pet. It is beyond my understanding.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat and underline that Castro is engaged in exporting revolution to Africa and inciting revolution in the Americas. People cannot understand why the government of Canada kowtows to Castro. The Prime Minister went to Cuba on an official visit. He said, "Castro, you wonderful fellow," while at the same time Castro had 10,000 or 12,000 troops in Africa undermining legitimate governments and spreading revolution. Today, if you speak to leading Americans both in and out of the administration, the first thing they will say is, "Why is Canada so close to Castro? Do you not know what he is doing?"
I will say no more about Castro except this: the fact that Canada's Prime Minister has placed Canada's arms around Castro is causing a deep sense of suspicion against Canada and its objectives all over the western world. I pass on to another example, France. France owes much to Canada. Its survival in two world wars is in very considerable measure due to the sacrifice of other countries and the soldiers of other countries. The treatment given to the government of Canada by the present administration of France is as unjustified as it is reprehensible. The French government encourages separation of Quebec from Canada.
Why has that been Canada's attitude? Why does Canada permit, without strong disapprobation and public disapprobation, the fact that the government of France and the administration in that country does everything they can in a subterranean and sometimes very open way to bring about the separation of Quebec from the Dominion of Canada.
December 20, 1977

What treatment has Canada received? Does this government fall in line with the present administration of France? The Hon. Gerard Pelletier was appointed Canadian ambassador to France. Normally, within a matter of a few days, an ambassador presents his letters of accreditation. What happened to him? He was in Paris for days and days. He wandered around the city of Paris and sometimes went out in the country. Since the minister made an observation a moment ago that I could not hear, I ask him whether he approves of the treatment given by France. Three weeks went by, almost four, and finally the government of France, the administration, accepted Pelletier with his letters of accreditation.
What happened to the Prime Minister of Canada? He went to Paris following the celebrations in London. He was invited to lunch with the President of France. That is a normal thing. How long did he have to wait? He was invited for lunch on a certain day. The President of France found he could not accommodate him that day and the date was postponed. That was an insult to Canada. I do not agree with the Prime Minister very often, but I found it difficult to understand the humility with which he was prepared to accept that insult, and yet the degree to which his sensibilities are aroused in the House of Commons if anyone in the opposition says anything even remotely critical of him.
Then Premier Levesque arrived and was met with pomp and circumstance. While Canada's practice for years has been that no foreign decoration be received by Canadians without the consent of the Canadian government, the President of France took Levesque in his arms and announced that he had been awarded the prestigious senior decoration, the Legion of Honour No. 1. He did not get the consent of the Canadian government.
What did the Canadian government do? Instead of taking objection the Prime Minister tried to laugh it off. From now on the rules respecting awards to Canadians by foreign governments will not require the consent of the Canadian government. Canadian after Canadian has had honours turned down from foreign countries. Surely France has not forgotten the tens of thousands of Canadians who gave their lives in two world wars.
What happened in this case was an insult to Canada, regardless to whom it occurs, and I will always take strong objection to it. The Prime Minister, in effect, said there was nothing Canada could do. Levesque did not wait for any consent: he started to wear it even before he got it.
Hear, hear!

We pass on from there. These are just indications of the degree to which this nation internationally is falling behind. I think of the announcement yesterday concerning South Africa. There was a tremendously courageous announcement! I was condemned because I took a stand at the Prime Ministers' Conference of 1960 and 1961 when an application was made by South Africa to rejoin the Commonwealth. The Prime Minister said today that I pushed South Africa out. He knew that statement was not true when he
External Affairs
made it. South Africa withdrew. It said it was through with the Commonwealth.
In 1960 I brought before the Prime Ministers' conference the proposition that if any country within the Commonwealth became a republic, but if later it decided that it wanted to be a member of the Commonwealth, to rejoin was not automatic. Such country should at least follow reasonably carefully those common dictates that activate men and women who believe in freedom. The debate, went on. I shall always remember it. I said to the Prime Minister of South Africa that all we ask is that South Africa shall not disfranchise 12 million or 13 million blacks. Under Botha and Smuts it was otherwise. The black and coloured had members. Those members were abolished. I said that I do not ask that you give man and man equality, but I ask you to restore the constituencies in the parliament of your country that prevailed for blacks or coloureds during the days of Field Marshal Jan Christian Smuts and General Botha. On and on went the argument.
In the passing years, the criticism of the stand I took has disappeared. Had 1 not taken that stand, the only white prime minister to take the stand at the Commonwealth, and had there been a vote, that would have been the end of the Commonwealth itself.
I was then criticized in this chamber. And holy of holies, the Liberal party was shocked into speech. They condemned me and said it was terrible. I always dislike missing observations which pass between outstanding and distinguished members of the government, and I am sorry that I missed that which passed just now between the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson)-because it must have been good.
The Deputy Prime Minister was writing speeches then.
He wrote the speeches condemning you.

I know he wrote one or two. I always enjoyed those which he wrote because they followed a common pattern. The identification was there without attribution.
Then the criticism of that day ceased in light of the recognition that had we had a vote in the Commonwealth at that time, that would have ended the institution. An announcement is now made in a rather surreptitious way. The government has a habit of doing this. Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs enunciated the government's policy toward South Africa. The minister normally does not assume the garland of self-imposed piety. I was not here yesterday, but having read what he said I thought he was a little apologetic. What of Canada's attitude? The western world has stood back and let Angola fall. Castro marched, or marched through others. Angola had the world's second largest diamond mines, diamonds which are so necessary today to modern production. We are now going to cut off South Africa, or at least go so far as we can. It has the world's largest production of diamonds, manganese and chromium.

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
This brings me to the situation today in Rhodesia. Rhodesia produces 14 per cent, I think, of the world's supply of chromium. If Rhodesia falls, the U.S.S.R. or its sycophants will control 93 per cent of the world's chromium. Are we going to cut off trade with South Africa? No, Mr. Speaker. Today the Prime Minister did a mental somersault and said we are not going to do that. What we will be doing, Mr. Speaker, in effect, is driving South Africa, by isolation, more and more into the Russian orbit. The course that the government announced yesterday in such evanescent terms is to me a major policy blunder. Russia needs industrial diamonds. Russia now has access to Angola's wealth in this regard, but it is not sufficient. She will now find herself in the position of getting the necessary diamonds which she does not have now.
Why are we slapping South Africa in the face? In 1960 and 1961 the government was condemning me. Satan was spiritual compared to the description given of me for what I had done by taking a stand on behalf of freedom. Their memories have not failed them, Mr. Speaker. They remember the awful picture painted of the right hon. member for Prince Albert destroying the Commonwealth.
What is the situation today? All of the major supertankers, in their tripping from the Middle East, South Africa or North America, must use Capetown or Simontown for watering purposes. These are the two largest naval bases which can serve these major tankers. The United States navy uses the Simontown base for its submarine flotillas which patrol the bases there. These shipping routes are critically important. If they fall under the aegis, directly or indirectly, of the U.S.S.R., this is extremely dangerous to the survival of freedom not only there but throughout the world.
I make the appeal to the government to reconsider this question. I have not heard any hallelujah choruses from other parts of the world among our great allies. The course which was taken so cavalierly yesterday is one which is fraught with terrifying danger to the future of freedom everywhere in the world. I know the government will laugh it off. It will end up by saying that it has not done such a thing, that what it has done is for the benefit of South Africa or for some other country.
For Castro.

Castro does not come into this, but you would think he had been the government's adviser.
1 turn now to another matter. What has the government done on behalf of the millions and millions of people who love freedom as you and I, Mr. Speaker, love it? I speak of the Ukrainian people, the Baltic peoples and other peoples of smaller population than those two? Has it ever protested the treatment being handed out to the Ukrainians and to others in the United Nations? Never a word has been spoken since 1960. Why is that? Is that the way to establish world leadership-to be afraid to speak out?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Just before elections.

Somebody suggests the government will speak out just before elections. Well, the government has an awful lot of speaking to do if it thinks it is going to survive. Canada has not spoken out since September, 1960, when on behalf of the nation, with Khrushchev present, I protested strongly against denial of freedom in the Ukraine. And do not tell me that protests are ineffective. The Kremlin does react to international criticism. I call as my witness in that behalf Cardinal Slipyj, who for many years, I think 17, was a prisoner often in solitary confinement in labour camps in Siberia. He was in Canada three years ago and was asked about the protest that was made by the former prime minister of Canada, John Diefenbaker. He said, "I have been in solitary confinement for more than 19 months, and others who loved freedom as I do are in the same position." Suddenly, one day in late September, 1960, we found that an amelioration took place. The U.S.S.R. does react to criticism. It did in that case.
What about the United Nations today? It seems quarantined against adopting protests and resolutions concerning the denial of fundamental freedoms and the tyranny being practised at this very moment toward freedom-loving citizens under the control of the U.S.S.R. No action can be taken in that forum. I call as my first witness at this point the Ukrainian Committee, a body which has made a tremendous contribution to freedom over the years. In 1970, 1971 and 1972 they got in touch with the Secretary-General of the United Nations concerning the terrible injustices being done to Ukrainians- and this applies to 50 million others who are behind the Iron Curtain. The protest was not even submitted to the assembly. But the Kremlin does feel criticism. It does react. I hope that the heart of this government will be moved even now to protest against the awfulness of the tyranny being perpetrated against these people.
Hear, hear!

Or does freedom know double standards?
Is the standard of this government the standard of Canada? Not at all. 1 go across this country and one of the major criticisms I hear is this: the government is frozen in its own image of self-importance and refuses to do anything internationally unless forced to do so. Mr. Speaker, I fear for the continuance of the United Nations. I do not see how it can stand up having regard to some of the things it has done or failed to do in the last year or so. I believe I am the only member of this House who was in San Francisco in 1945. I sat two seats behind that great tribune Field-Marshal Smuts, the only person there who had been a member of the original League of Nations. He said, "I wonder if this organization will go the way of the League of Nations." I see the United Nations today becoming dominated by small individual states who are united by only one thing-a common desire to achieve their own objectives. I fear that unless one of the great nations like Canada speaks out, the United Nations is on the road to suicide.
December 20, 1977

What of the millions who are in the camps? I saw the statement made the other day by the Prime Minister. Ele said he was disturbed by the fate of these millions. What about the thousands of freedom-loving dissidents who, like Valentyn Moroz, are imprisoned over there and held without evidence whatever? What about the tens of thousands who have been in prison camps and mental hospitals? Although unidentified, they belong to the immortals in freedom's lexicon.
Mr. Speaker, I am told my time is almost up and therefore I want to pass on to just one other observation. I want to deal with the general situation as 1 find it. Here we are, meeting in this chamber in complete quietness and calm. How few today have spoken out against the overwhelming power in military terms and the growing threat presented by the Soviet ballistic-missile navy? This is an hour of peril. Admiral Douglas Boyle stated recently that there are 32 missiles at sea in Soviet submarines in the Atlantic within range of Chicago, 24 within range of the whole of North America, and 32 in the Pacific within range of American missile sites in the west. According to the Admiral, the Soviets will have 30 of their Delta-class submarines in commission before the U.S. Navy equivalent Trident-class boat is launched. Mr. Speaker, we are living in a period of calm similar to that which characterized Europe during the period from 1934 to 1939. Only Churchill then spoke out. He was regarded as a pariah. He was a voice in the wilderness. I heard him speak on two occasions: the House emptied. He said the war was coming, but nobody paid attention.
On March 24 of this year General Alexander Haig said the Russian offensive build-up was "unimaginably" greater than had been expected. Major-General George J. Keegan of U.S. Air Force Intelligence said that for 25 years the U.S. Secret Service underrated what was happening. Yet here we are, doing nothing, living in a fool's paradise. Everywhere, all over the world, the U.S.S.R. is marching-not with its own troops but with those of other nations. The only warning from one of the great powers has come from the Chinese. They warn that the Russians plan the military take-over of western Europe and go on to say it could be completed within 21 days without serious damage to western industry. South Africa and the Middle East would then be taken over in a matter of days.
Some may ask me: Why has Russia not struck? Mr. Speaker, I have read every work which had been published on this subject in the last ten years. Most conclude with that question. 1 think the answer is this: the Kremlin is afraid of its own dissidents. The United States cannot understand Canada's attitude. Indeed, to a very great extent today the United States does not trust the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Ridiculous!
Why should they?
I heard someone say "Ridiculous". Oh, it is all right to laugh it off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is that what you want?

The interruptor at the back there is fully qualified by his lack of intelligence. I make that statement advisedly. Why has Canada carried on as it has with Castro? Did the United States approve? It was and is deeply concerned.
Oh, oh!
The hon. member is qualified by his ignorance to keep quiet.
What do you mean by that?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), but his allotted time has expired. Nevertheless, he may continue if there is unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.
The hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos) has no knowledge of the subject at all, yet he said "No". One member can do that in this House.
The hon. member should not have insulted the minister. .
It is a shame the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos) is such a child and cannot accept some criticism in this House. He should be sent back to the Department of External Affairs.
No, that cannot be done.

Mr. Speaker, although I follow the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the debate, needless to say I will not follow him in his style nor in his convictions in certain matters. I listened with great interest to the right hon. member. It was one of his more entertaining speeches. Occasionally I wondered whether the right hon. member was dealing with the issues from the point of view of self-justification or whether he was dealing with the issues as they appear in the world today.
Particularly I was struck by his references to South Africa. The right hon. member spent a good deal of his time talking about the moral stature which Canada ought to have in the world. Also, he indicated that Canada ought to be interested in the grievances of Ukrainians and the Balkans. He felt Canada should stand up for the rights of people throughout the world. I agree entirely.
Hear, hear!

But when the right hon. member referred to South Africa, his standards changed. I hope he will look carefully at the words he used in the debate today. He seemed to indicate that Canada should not participate with other

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
countries in disciplining the government of South Africa which is engaged in an abhorrent policy.
Just like Uganda.

1 do not intend to follow this line. 1 am grateful to the right hon. member for suggesting a debate on foreign affairs. However, I am surprised he did not deal with some of the more fundamental issues facing the world, rather than personally attacking the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This debate provides me with an opportunity to congratulate my successors in the office of the secretary of state for external affairs, the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and his predecessor, the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen). If the Deputy Prime Minister was not such a superb House leader, probably he would still be the secretary of state for external affairs.
Oh, oh!
How does that make you feel, Don?
As a Newfoundlander, I resent that.

The Deputy Prime Minister was disappointed when the Prime Minister asked him to revert to his old job as House leader. But I realize I speak for everyone in the House when 1 say that those who take an interest in foreign affairs are full of admiration for the manner in which the Deputy Prime Minister brought his great talents to bear in the field of Canada's external relations. The best evidence of his judgment and skill in this field was how he handled the co-chairmanship of the north-south dialogue. It was agreed, had it not been for his patience and negotiating skills, that the conference probably would have been a total failure. Second was his selection, as Canadian negotiator of the northern pipeline agreement with the United States, which is one of the most important agreements in our generation.
The hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs has talents of a different kind. Those talents stand him in good stead. I am happy this man is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He has taken over his responsibility with skill and imagination. On many occasions I have listened to him answering questions posed by members opposite, and I have admiration for the way he commands his department and is knowledgeable of this intricate field. I am sure all hon. members wish him well. He has a balance of common sense which derives from his origin and his background. He has a sense of idealism which will stand him in good stead in the turmoil of this rapidly changing world.
When I was the secretary of state for external affairs, I proceeded on the premise that a foreign policy should, as far as possible, be non-partisan. I believed then, as I do now, that Canada can achieve its external objectives most effectively if there is a broad measure of agreement among all parties. This does not mean that the opposition should agree at all times as to how the government proceeds to achieve its objectives. There is plenty of room for criticism, even if there is broad agreement on objectives.

I have listened to the various speakers who have participated in this debate, as well as reading their speeches. I should like to make some remarks to illustrate how much agreement exists on the basic element of Canada's foreign policy. No one has questioned Canada's membership in NATO, nor the presence of Canadian troops in Europe. Speakers for the official opposition have urged that we should support NATO more. No one has questioned Canada's responsibility to provide development assistance. The criticism is that Canada is not doing enough.
Party spokesmen vied with one another in their commitment to the defence of human rights throughout the world. Doubts were expressed about the implementation of the third option in our relations with the United States, as well as the contractual link in relation with the European community. But no spokesman has disagreed with the purpose of these policies or principles. The Commonwealth, which our Prime Minister has done so much to sustain, is still considered to be a useful instrument for the promotion of international understanding. All parties voiced approval of the additional measures announced by the minister to show Canada's disapproval of apartheid in South Africa, with the exception of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who apparently does not speak on behalf of his party in this case.
All members joined the minister in welcoming the recent dramatic moves for peace in the Middle East. Whatever differences there may be about the details of nuclear safeguards which Canada is attempting to apply, there is no difference among the parties on the essentiality of preventing the geographical proliferation of nuclear weapons. On that we are all agreed. If I may say so, this is not surprising. Canadian foreign policy is not an ideological matter, it is not the product of the imagination of particular foreign ministers who happened to be in office at the time the foreign policy of Canada is derived from certain basic and unalterable facts. The first of them is our geographical position in the world. I can remember on one occasion being in the Canadian embassy in the Soviet Union when the then foreign minister, Lester Pearson, was making a speech. He was thanking our Russian hosts for their hospitality. We had made our first visit to the Soviet Union at the beginning of the fall, and he was addressing three of the big five who were then in office.
He said that Canada is not a big country, that we have a lot of geography, we do not have many people and we do not have a long history, but we occupy a strategic position in the world, located as we are between the United States in the south and the Soviet Union in the north, and therefore are subject to pressures from both sides, to which Mr. Kaganovitch-who was then one of the Russian leaders-rose and said that so far as the Soviet Union is concerned, it is friendly pressure. Mr. Pearson then replied-and I am sure the right hon. gentleman would agree with him in that respect-that the strongest pressure he knew was friendly pressure.
So it is our geographical position in the world that has a profound effect upon Canadian foreign policy. The second is
December 20, 1977

our history, and particularly our peaceful evolution to independence. Not many countries can say they have not had major wars or revolutions in their territories, but we can say that and it has a strong influence on our foreign policy. Our dependence for domestic prosperity on trade, which arises from our resources and our position in the world, is another fact which influences Canadian foreign policy. Another is the origins of the people who make up this country, drawn from all over the world, and our full commitment to democracy and freedom.
These facts have led all governments, the government under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the government of Mr. Louis St. Laurent, the government of Mackenzie King, the government of Mr. Pearson and the present government, to very similar conclusions. I was very interested to find, when I was listening to the right hon. gentleman, that he never dealt with any of these fundamental issues. He dealt, in a very entertaining and striking way, with what were really the superficial aspects of Canadian foreign policy and I think he missed a great opportunity, but of course that is his business.
May I now turn for a few minutes to a particular application of the principle of a non-partisan approach to foreign policy which I think is important, that is, the relation to the activities of members of parliament when they go abroad on interparliamentary visits. As hon. members are aware, there are now innumerable interparliamentary gatherings, and I understand from Mr. Speaker that there are others waiting to be formed. For the first time in my experience in the House of Commons,
I had the honour of co-chairing the Canadian side of one of these interparliamentary bodies, namely, the Canadian European Parliamentary Association. This has given me a new insight into some of the problems and opportunities associated with these institutions, even though as secretary of state for external affairs I had some knowledge because 1 was consulted about them from time to time.
Their most beneficial aspect is the opportunity to exchange views on problems of common concern, and this exchange can be superficial or it can be in depth, depending entirely on the personnel on both sides of these discussions and their willingness and ability to participate. My first observation arising from this recent experience is that although there has been in recent years a considerable improvement in the preparedness of Canadian parliamentarians to participate at these interparliamentary meetings, we can do much better. We still do not take these contacts seriously enough, to the detriment of Canada's position in the world and Canada's relations with other countries.
One reason for this is that Canadian parliamentarians, unless they have ministerial experience, parliamentary secretaries or active members of committees concerned with external affairs, do not become very expert in the subjects on which they are talking to parliamentarians from other countries, except of course in domestic matters on which they may be truly experts. I know that briefings by officials are helpful, but there is not the continuity sometimes that is desirable in these contacts.
External Affairs
The school for members of parliament in external relations should be the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, but I regret to say that recently it has not been fulfilling that role, a role which I think would be very useful. When I was secretary of state for external affairs I found it very useful to refer matters of importance in foreign policy to that committee, but more recently, for reasons that I do not quite understand, there has been considerable devolution in the activities of that committee.
I have in front of me a list of inquiries that were undertaken by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, beginning in 1968. There was one inquiry in 1968, one in 1969, and six in 1970, there were four in 1971, one in 1972, four in 1973, two in 1974, and in each of the last three years only one. 1 am excluding the consideration of the estimates. What I am talking about are full-scale inquiries arising out of the estimates, or out of a reference of a piece of legislation. It seems to me that it would be very desirable that this committee be reactivated and given more work, because I cannot believe that there are no problems that could be referred to the committee.

May 1 ask the hon. member a question? Would he not agree that combining national defence and foreign affairs with some of the problems that have existed in national defence since the so-called unification has tended to put external affairs questions somewhat on the back burner?

I do not know that 1 agree altogether with that. 1 would have thought there are some questions that could have been discussed in that committee, such as some that were discussed in this debate, where there might have been a better opportunity for an exchange of views, for bringing in people to bring testimony, and so forth, purely on questions of external affairs and not only on national defence. In making these comments, you will see that I am following the tradition of being non-partisan. I do not mind raising questions of this kind which 1 think are important to the functioning of this institution.
Another reason for the relevant ineffectiveness is that the Canadian side of interparliamentary associations, or at least the elected members from this side, do not report to anybody, either to the House or to a standing committee. Recently I had the experience of being co-chairman of the Canada European Parliamentary Association which underlined the curious position of the Canadian side. With the approval of Mr. Speaker, a subcommittee was formed to examine more closely relations between Canada and the EEC with respect to nuclear energy.
At the conclusion of our subcommittee discussions which took place first in Brussels and then in Ottawa, the European side insisted upon the preparation of a communique or a report which they wished to make to their parent body, the European parliament, so we agreed to the preparation of a report-but I had nowhere to send it. I gave it to Mr. Speaker, who was the

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
only authority I could find who could receive this report. I sent copies for information purposes to the committee, which is now defunct but one will understand the problems which arose. This was an important report which should have been referred to a standing committee for discussion. At least it ought to have appeared in print. As it is now, it resides in Mr. Speaker's hands and in the hands of the members of the committee for their information, but I have no machinery for its transmission.

Mr. Speaker, 1 point out that when I was co-chairman of the Canada-U.S. delegation some years ago, along with my successor as Speaker we were able to convince the then Mr. Speaker Lamoureux to table the report so that it would appear as an appendix to Hansard. This was done as a result of my insistence, so the precedent is there. 1 wish the hon. member well in his efforts to get those printed as appendices. The hon. member should just try it and see how far he gets.

I thank the hon. gentleman. That does not solve all the problems, however, because in this particular case it was a subcommittee; it was not the committee as a whole. There might have been greater ease in getting the House to agree to publish the report of the committee, but this was the report of a subcommittee and this multiplied the problems. However, I thank the hon. gentleman. 1 think his heart is in the same place as mine, he wants to see these procedures improved.
When Canadian parliamentarians meet their counterparts from other countries, they are not participating in negotiations. That is the function of the governments of Canada and the other countries concerned, but by such activities Canadian parliamentarians are engaged in promoting understanding, and this requires them, on the one hand, to be as fully aware as possible of the policies of the Canadian government. On the other hand, they must be able to report their activities and conclusions to the body from which they were selected. After all, these meetings have a purpose other than educating individual members of parliament. 1 therefore suggest that at an appropriate time we ought to look at our standing rules.
At one time the idea that there should be a report to the House was put forward. I am not quite sure whether I would think that desirable, because 1 think it would be resisted very strongly by those who have the responsibility for organizing the work of the House. However, I see no reason why the report should not be referred automatically to a standing committee and provide the basis for further discussion if that is desired.
Hear, hear!

At least the reports would then have a place to appear.
I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is listening when I say I think our friends in the other place have better facilities and do a somewhat better job than we do in this field. These reports are usually printed in

Hansard for the other place. The standing committee on foreign affairs of the other place prepares excellent reports on Canadian-European relations and Canadian-American relations. We have not yet been able to match those reports in thoroughness or in quality, and I as a member of the House of Commons somewhat resent the fact that I have to admit to the co-chairman of my committee that he is in a better position to handle these matters than I am as the co-chairman from the House of Commons.
In concluding these very general remarks, I would like to make some suggestions. 1 suggest that Canadian external policy should continue to be non-partisan in character, or at least as non-partisan as it can be; that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence be encouraged to become more active by suitable references moved by the ministry; that care be taken in the representation of the House in interparliamentary groups and in the briefing and preparation for meetings; and that reports from parliamentary meetings be referred automatically to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence or to any other standing committee which may be appropriate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I listened with great interest to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp). I am reminded of a question I asked the government House leader yesterday with respect to possible activity in the coming period of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. 1 understand that some discussions were to take place. 1 know this was on the mind of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. Have those discussions taken place?
No, not yet.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate on external affairs. Although not an expert in the subject, since my early childhood I have always been interested in what may happen throughout the world, and this passion has not diminished since I have been elected. When we travel throughout the world and see how people and citizens of the various countries welcome Canadian delegates, I can tell that it is heartening to be a Canadian, with the consideration we receive everywhere in the world.
The very quick advent of communications had the effect of reducing the size of the earth and of bringing closer, at least theoretically, the peoples and the nations. Today we cannot ignore the problems faced by some nations and individuals several thousands of miles away from our home. Not only should we become aware of these problems but it is also our duty to react and give if necessary, while respecting the sovereignty of each country, the help and the support, and in this regard the action of the Canadian Armed Forces in the peace force of the United Nations is exemplary. On the other hand, we cannot help regretting that such a measure is always followed by a conflict, that it comes always too late in reality. Prevention is better than cure. I think a peace policy should
December 20, 1977

always be oriented in a preventive direction. It is obvious that intervention after the facts is not bad in itself if it is the only solution. I am sure that with a little foresight and courage we could prevent some conflicts.
It is not a secret for anybody that for over 30 years the world has been divided into two, a Russian camp, and an American camp. Nearly all other countries are following behind either of these superpowers and, unfortunately, Canada is no exception. The so-called non-aligned countries are trying more or less successfully to maintain some sort of neutrality, but silence is sometimes more eloquent than a flow of words.
As far as Third World countries are concerned, it is clear that we are witnessing the emergence of a new political force in the world. Its current lack of unity and cohesion, however, prevents it from playing its legitimate part on the world scene, but this is only temporary and is likely to change entirely the rules of the game. As I was saying, for all practical purposes the world is divided into two camps. China, in spite of its recent opening to the outside world, is an unknown quantity which remains quite mysterious. There are no conflicts in which its two adversaries are not fighting one another through third parties. Up to a point, this is a good thing, for a direct confrontation between them would certainly mean the end of civilization on earth. On the other hand, it is revolting to see the great powers manipulating and encouraging countries and people in conflict in order to consolidate their zone of influence. It is the duty of Canada impartially to denounce such practices by great powers.
One of the areas where Canada could play the part of a watchdog is that of armament sales. It is mainly by this means that the great powers keep alive the disputes of the small countries. A recent article of the Monde diplomatique dealing with the delivery of weapons to foreign countries was very revealing on this point. In 1976, the United States sales of armaments abroad came to $9.5 billion. This is 25 per cent of the national income of Canada for the same year. But what is even more alarming is that nearly $8 billion of these $9.5 billion were sales to developing countries. Perhaps the United States did not force these countries to buy arms, but then they did not dissuade them either. In any case, had the United States not responded to their requests, these underdeveloped countries would have turned towards the U.S.S.R which would have been eager to satisfy them.
We must admit that these countries very often have dictatorial or repressive regimes and that they play the game called by the great powers which take advantage of their servility. Meanwhile, the people of these countries still live in poverty and are deprived of genuine freedom. That is what Canada must denounce, not to achieve a comfortable place for itself but to bring about respect for individual liberties. During this year of "the political prisoner", the subject of individual liberties has been talked about very often. But talking about it is just not enough; we must take steps to ensure that every individual in every country has an equal opportunity to live
External Affairs
these liberties and above all, to understand them. It is well known that the Helsinki Conference has been used by the U.S.S.R. as a smokescreen of good will so it would be put to better use within the Russian frontiers. This year, the surveillance group established in May 1976 in Moscow with a mandate to seek respect for human rights has been destroyed in the repression. In Czechoslovakia, for instance, the signatories and supporters of "Charter 77" who only asked for the implementation of the Helsinki Final Act provisions were subject to harsh repression. This repression took the forms of arrests, questioning, layoffs and even legal proceedings. Most western countries have categorically although very politely condemned such actions which are simply undermining a little more the bases of an already very precarious freedom. Surely enough, in such cases governments are bound to adopt a very diplomatic approach because we maintain important trading relations with them. Besides, the sovereignty of countries over domestic problems is unquestionable. However, there are cases where we must rise and protest as strongly as possible because this principle is a basic right and as such we are collectively responsible for it.
But the serious situation in eastern countries should not lull us into forgetting human rights in other countries which are under American control. In countries like Chile and Argentina, the freedoms of expression and thought are hardly better respected than in the U.S.S.R. Let us not forget that it is thanks to the help at the U.S. that a democratically elected government was defeated in Chile. Let us not forget either that the police forces of these countries which are known for their very liberal use of torture and unexplained disappearances have been trained in the United States.
As far as South Africa and Rhodesia are concerned, the situation speaks for itself. Under the cover of advanced countries, these two nations maintain some of the most repressive regimes in the world. If our foreign policy were to be fair, we should condemn every threat to individual freedom, no matter in what country such repression takes place. Our credibility towards all the people under the yoke of oppression is at stake.
Mr. Speaker, the particular situation of Canada as opposed to the countries of the Third World is a matter of opinion. On one hand, Canada is among industrialized countries because of its geographical situation, its standard of living and its culture. On the other hand, however, being an exporter of raw materials, it also finds itself on the other side of the fence, among underdeveloped countries.
Just like the Third World countries, Canada is under the economic domination of the United States in the sense that it exports its raw materials towards that country which returns them as finished products. As in the case of the underdeveloped countries, large American multinationals exploit our natural resources and make huge profits out of them, and as one speaks of economic dependency, one implies a political counterpart, so that we are finding ourselves pretty well in the same situation as these small countries. So it seems to me that a particular link should unite Canada to these countries since to some extent we experience the same problems. As I was just

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
saying, the Third World will undoubtedly soon become a major international political force.
The day when underdeveloped countries will decide to ask a fair price for their materials which developed nations need so badly, we will witness a drastic reversal of the situation. We must open our eyes and our minds to examine thoroughly these issues so as to realize that we must take right here in Canada all available means to promote a better understanding between governments and nations of the world, so that one day we do not find ourselves at a disadvantage.
We do not want to have situations we could not accept and not take steps to try not to impose such situations on other countries as well. This movement I just mentioned is already shaping up, and all it lacks to go is unity, a coherence that it does not have now; they are still divided, but they will manage to create that unity overnight. They have created a very powerful economic and political force in the world and let us hope that we will not be the target of the oppression movements against the peoples that they now consider as not helping them but working against them.
We can certainly not rely on the great capitalistic powers to consolidate that movement. They have too much to lose. On the other hand, a country like Canada in the privileged situation it occupies can provide that leadership. To do that, it must clearly take sides with the small people, those who are tired of external domination and want to take their destiny in their own hands without any interference from the great powers.
IVliss Begin: There are always some of those.

What we must aim for-and 1 will answer the minister-is a fair and equitable redistribution of wealth at both international and national levels. This does not mean we must declare war against the capitalist countries but quite simply that they-and Canada, to a lesser extent- will have to pay the fair price for what they take. Situations change in the world. So let us be careful and enlightened and realize that that situation could change at any moment. In any case, even if Canada does not take part in that movement, it will happen sooner or later. Canada's participation can only make it happen faster. The balance will be reset one day or the other, and Canada should take part in that movement instead of being caught off-guard. Mr. Speaker, 1 will say that Canadians can be rather proud of Canada's external policy. In general, whatever the government, Canada's external policy has been one of conciliation and generosity toward underdeveloped countries-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Liberals have been here for a few years!

I would not want the hon. member for Chambly (Mr. Loiselle) to believe that that is the financial contribution of the Liberal Party, for that is the contribution of the whole nation. So, it does not matter if that

was under the Liberal or the Progressive Conservative government. That might have been the same also under a good Social Credit government, for the nation does not belong to any party and the parties must serve the nation. That is how I see politics.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is what we are in power for!

The hon. member for Chambly says: That is what we are in power for. Do you want to show that you are in power? You have the majority, as 1 have said time and time again, you have the majority of the seats, but the real power is outside the House. It is in the hands of national and international high finance. You are nothing but servants of financiers.
Mr. Speaker, since Canada is not a great power, it is listened to with less cynicism than the other developed countries. All of that is to its benefit and it should take advantage of the situation to promote a more equitable order around the world. Canada can and must play a middle-man role in the various conflicts. It must also entertain a favourable attitude toward disadvantaged countries. When as a delegate of this Parliament I had the opportunity of travelling officially to Cyprus for instance and visiting parts of that island including Nicosia and other towns, I noticed that among the UN Forces present there, it is toward the Canadians that the population felt most respect. It was also in the occupied sector patrolled by Canadians where things were more peaceful and where the fewest incidents ever occurred.
So in my opinion Canada is meeting its obligations in this role. It also plays a crucial role in trying to preserve peace in these areas. Yet Canada is capable of doing more. It can set a good example by participating in all conferences in order to bring about a better understanding in the world about the riches which God gave the earth and which are at the disposal of all nations. It is the duty of every government to see to it that their population benefits from economic and social policies which will provide for a better distribution throughout the world so as to better satisfy human needs, thereby fostering a spirit of conciliation among nations. So much the better, Mr. Speaker, if this can be achieved. One must not forget that before any armed conflict, before any war is declared, there are economic wars being waged. There is a continuing economic war for the conquest of markets and it is now going on since every industrialized country wants to export its surpluses outside so as to ensure a steady production and provide employment for its residents. You just have to read the newspaper reports, especially those from Europe. We are confronted by a situation that has been experienced before the 1939-45 war and those who write the history of their people remind us about these issues that these armed conflicts have always been provoked and preceded by an economic war for the conquest of markets.
I am convinced that this debate has been carried out quite objectively, despite the few incidents that took place and the odd rivalries between the various ministers who have to preside
December 20, 1977

over the destiny of our country in the field of foreign affairs yet, over all, this has been a time for reflection.
