speakeroldname: Mr. Dan McKenzie (Winnipeg South Centre) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-217, to amend the Broadcasting Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as this will be one of the last pieces of major legislation to be debated in the House in 1977, I hope that it receives approval from the government and is allowed to go to committee. Canada's educators, the universities and schools, have been fighting this for some eight years. We hope some headway will be made today.
1 speak on behalf of six million students in Canada in schools and universities and 250,000 teachers and school trustees who have been pressing for some action on this bill for the past five years. We hope the government has its heart in the right place today, seeing it is Christmas. This will be an opportunity to wish Canada's six million students a very merry Christmas and 250,000 teachers and school trustees a happy New Year by passing this bill and sending it to committee.
In retrospect, perhaps the wording of the bill should have been different. The bill provides that only school boards, as opposed to any publicly-supported educational institution, be given access to CBC productions. The bill also provides that any material deemed to have educational content be made available free rather than at a nominal or specified charge. In spite of these two oversights, however, the rationale behind the bill is clear. If there are any technical or legal aspects to be dealt with, they could be attended to in committee.

Stand.

December 20, 1977
Broadcasting Act
The current situation with regard to the accessibility of CBC broadcast materials is incredible. Network materials, often so splendidly produced and so useful for educational purposes, lie buried in vaults. Canadian educators should be able to take CBC educational materials obtained through the library service of the CBC or its commercial outlet, Visual Education Centre Inc., or obtained directly off the air from radio or television at the time of the broadcast, or taped off-air from radio and television for use at some other time, either free of charge or at minimal cost. These materials would be used in schools and universities only on a strictly non-profit basis.
In October, 1975, the then secretary of state announced that CBC programs would be available for post-broadcast use. This is only a partial solution to the problems with which my bill deals. There is very limited value to post-broadcast films.
The present Broadcasting Act is outmoded and inapplicable to today's technological and educational process. Teachers are inhibited by the present Broadcasting Act from fully realizing the potential of the technology available to them and to their students. Public school systems constitute a distinct and identifiable group within which access to materials can be planned and accounted for. Teachers and students should have access to as wide a range of materials as possible in order to ensure the highest quality of education. Copying and duplicating should be allowed for, subject to suitable safeguards to protect the legitimate interests of the creator and publisher.
In the case of broadcast programs of an educational nature, there should be recognition of the need to record these for playback within a limited period. In this situation, the tape recording may be used to meet timetabling contingencies without royalty payment. Transmission of copyright material through closed circuit television systems should be subject to reasonable royalties and fees in terms of the specific target audience. School boards and teachers have experienced distress in recent months because of current inadequacies in legislation and agreement at the federal level. Threats of legal suit have been made. While I am aware of the complexity of what is involved, meaningful action at the federal level is needed.
As for control, teachers' associations and school boards have stated that they would control the use of productions considered educational, and that the school board would determine what productions are educational. They would do so upon the recommendation of their teaching staff. The school boards would be prepared to report to the CBC productions used for educational purposes. Basically, all they are asking for is in the interests of the six million children and young people in the schools of this country. We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that they are the future. They are the future MPs, MLAs, the future creators of intellectual property, the future CBC staff and officers, the future teachers and trustees. They are important people.
I received a letter from the Association of Canadian Television and Radio Artists, based in Toronto, forwarding to me for information regarding education. ACTRA states that it is in

close association with teacher and professor groups nationally, and in several provinces is active in developing working agreements that govern the production of materials to be used in education. It is greatly concerned that careful attention be paid, in the development of public policy in this field, to the needs of the creators of these materials.
Suggestions have been made in the past few years that certain kinds of educational" materials-one example is programs made for the CBC-should be more widely available for use in schools, colleges and universities, and also for wider educational purposes, including broadcasting. "Education" used in this fashion has no practical meaning, beyond "wide use". They enthusiastically support this wide use, and indeed are doing everything they can to ensure that Canadian materials of all kinds are available for use by our educators and others.
At the same time, they do not believe the public will be best served if these materials are made available without certain controls-controls that protect a creator's moral rights in his work and that ensure he will be paid fairly for the use of that work. It is particularly important that the revised Copyright Act does not make any provisions that exclude materials used for education from copyright control, or that any action is taken to force the CBC or any other agency either to give away its materials or to allow their use without making fair payment to the creators of those programs.
I have also been in communication with the Canadian School Trustees' Association regarding some of the points dealt with by the bill and the desirability of passing such a bill to committee. May I put on the record some of the recommendations they make. They have this to say:
The Council for Educational Technology in England has written to CSTA and said, "As for broadcasts intended for schools and for adult and further education, these may be recorded off air and retained for three years." If it can be done in England-why not in Canada?
I hope the parliamentary secretary will have good news this evening in this regard. If they have worked out the problems in England in regard to obtaining educational films, and I do not see why we in Canada cannot find a solution. They continue:
Both the BBC and the Independent Television Companies Association Limited (the equivalent to CTV in Canada) have forms of agreements with educational authorities (the equivalents to school boards in Canada) to permit off-air televising.
The CBC has been studying British systems, around about the time that you had another bill of similar nature before the House, but they apparently were ahead of the arrangements in Britain which came about in 1975-or they knew of them and wanted no part of them.
The Canadian Teachers' Federation and the Canadian School Trustees' Association supported your bill, and they represent some 250,000 people in Canada, around 6,000 of whom are elected men and women in the same manner as MPs. Their views must have some impact on MPs if they are representing their constituencies effectively.
Further, the Canadian Parent-Teacher, Home and School Federation also supported your efforts and they represent even greater numbers of constituents across Canada.
That is an indication of just how many people we are speaking about this afternoon.
December 20, 1977

As for authors, composers, actors, etc.-why do they hesitate, if they do? They need circulation of their materials, especially Canadian authors, composers, actors, etc.-your bill will help them, not cheat them of some money. Besides, the CBC and CTV are good pay right now-Canadian creators are not being cheated.
Trustees, teachers, home and school have repeatedly urged more Canadian content in curriculum and educational materials. Your bill will encourage such desired activity because of the additional exposure to students in the classrooms and to teachers who will want to use the materials.
Writers, composers, musicians, etc. receive copyright protection through the efforts of the Canadian taxpayers. Is it unreasonable to ask them to find some accommodation for students in classrooms to benefit from their works by off-air recording for classroom use?
The Canadian School Trustees' Association tells me that their membership has agreed to a form of licensing and an annual reasonable fee to provide for taping off-air and other copyright considerations. The moneys earned, if matched by the Canada Council, would provide considerable funds for Canadian authors, musicians, etc.
Finally, your constituents want such privileges for schools as being able to tape off-air, such as they can in Britain and have told you so in the past by letter, personal contact, and telegram. It will not be costly to do so; all that is necessary is to respond to a very reasonable request of our constituents-one which, for a change, will not cost an arm and a leg.
This is the letter I have received from Mr. C. H. Witney, an executive director of CSDA. 1 also have a copy of a letter from Mr. R. S. Ingram, the secretary-treasurer of School District No. 63 (Saanich), British Columbia. He draws attention to the cost of the video equipment they installed in the schools. He states:
Twenty thousand dollars have been spent to date on the receiver-monitor equipment in our district. This equipment cannot be used to its full potential because of the exorbitant cost of acquiring video tape.
A number of schools across Canada have invested in this video closed circuit TV equipment and it has proved to be of very little use or of no use at all. The letter goes on to point out that suitable video tapes are not available from the CBC due to video educational centre involvement in connection with single performance use of such tapes. The cost, the writer says, is prohibitive because of union agreements calling for $73 for one artist, single use, and a PEMC agreement with script writers. The cost would be $547 for a half-hour script or $1,094 for a half-hour script with copyright. These fees are, of course, exorbitant. They are much too high for the school boards to afford. I am sure this aspect could be discussed in committee. I have with me, also, a letter from Mr. N. J. Parker-Jervis, of the Department of English at the University of Alberta. He says:
I have much to do with the audio-visual centre run by the English department here and I, too, am much concerned with the questions you raise. For years, it seems to me, 1 have been lobbying, particularly with the CBC and the BBC, to persuade them to tackle the problem of copyright and residuals. I have not met with much success. The network materials often so splendidly produced and so useful for educational purposes lie buried in vaults.
Let us hope we have some success today. Let us bring this material out of the vaults. I have also received letters on the subject from the Canadian Home and School and Parent-Teachers Federation, an influential organization which takes an interest in the subject and whose office is in Toronto. I have received further correspondence from Mr. Victor Dotten, past-
Broadcasting Act
president of the federation. 1 first introduced this bill in the last parliament. After a lot of letter-writing, representations to ministers and so forth, the government agreed to send the subject matter to a committee if 1 would withdraw the measure. I did withdraw my bill and the subject was referred to a committee. On Tuesday, May 7, 1974, 1 attended a committee meeting with six other Conservatives. The only person present from the government side was the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart). A couple of CBC officials were there, along with a representative of the School Trustees' Association and representatives of the Canadian Teachers' Federation who had come from British Columbia, the maritimes and central Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that meeting had to be called off because of the absence of all-party representation. No Liberals showed up. It was one of the most contemptuous things I have seen since I arrived in Ottawa. The first meeting was held at 3.30 in the afternoon. The hon. member for Cochrane said we would call the meeting once again for eight o'clock that evening. I attended once again at eight o'clock, along with the school trustees and six of my Conservative colleagues. We walked into an empty room. Even the chairman was not there. That is a contemptuous way to treat people, but it is characteristic of the manner in which the government has dealt with the situation for the last eight years. I believe the people on whose behalf I am speaking are making a legitimate request and deserve decisive answers. I hope the parliamentary secretary will not stand up today and read some reply which a civil servant has prepared to this important question. I trust we shall hear some pleasant words from the spokesman for the government on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not comment on the hon. member's statement about the government taking a contemptuous attitude, because I am not really sure this was the case. However, I have a certain amount of sympathy with this bill because it is an attempt to help schools and boards of education, and as a former chairman of the Welland board of education I can understand the reason the bill has been introduced. In some ways, its objectives are praiseworthy, but as it stands it will be next to impossible to implement because of certain technical difficulties. Its introduction may help to smooth out the way to some financial assistance to educational bodies, but the difficulties to which I have referred remain. The Broadcasting Act provides, as the hon. member is aware, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation establish a service which is varied and sometimes all encompassing. I draw particular attention to the fact that the corporation-and I quote-is established for the purpose of providing the national broadcasting service contemplated under section 3 of the act. Under section 3(g) the national broadcasting service is defined as "a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportions."
I introduce the above to highlight the extent of the CBC's mandate and the practical limitations that budgets impose on

December 20, 1977
Broadcasting Act
objectives. In this respect, there are ever increasing demands being made on the CBC and its services with what often appears to be a total disregard with the latter's capability to respond effectively to the task at hand.
With these thoughts in mind, I would like to proceed to the examination of the legislation placed before the House and outline some of the ambiguities and conflicts inherent in the wording of Bill C-217. These are given here only when they affect the understanding of the intent. Referring to section 39(1 )(c) of Bill C-217, I note that the first proposed amendment would presumably require the CBC to at least give specific emphasis to some mechanism through which school boards throughout Canada could be given an opportunity to express their opinions as to the educational nature and value of the programs produced by or for the CBC. Assuming such a mechanism could be developed to the satisfaction of everyone concerned, this proposal still raises serious implications. First, to be effective, school boards would have to make their wishes known in advance of production or acquisition by the CBC. Negotiating for additional rights to a program that has been very well received by viewers can be difficult and costly. In some cases, whether or not a program has been acclaimed, clearances can take as long as a year following broadcast. It is always difficult and often impossible to judge the educational value of a program on the basis of a synopsis. Accordingly, school boards or their representatives would need a great deal of information about CBC production plans which typically are spread over a year or more before the broadcast date, and would want to see previews in some cases. As can justifiably be imagined, any such relationship would impose an impossible and unacceptable burden on production staffs. It would result in the widespread dissemination of highly confidential production information and would impose severe constraints in competing with other networks, particularly in current affairs and news.
Broadcasting programming is dynamic. It would be impossible to predict in advance of a program year what titles school boards might wish to deem educational. Clearing programs for post-broadcast use are expensive. More importantly, any arrangements through which school boards could be empowered to select CBC programs for post-broadcast use would make it possible for organizations chartered under provincial legislation to make relatively open-ended demands against the corporation's operating budgets approved in parliament.
The hon. member no doubt will attest to the constitutional problems and difficulties at issue in this approach. They are given further emphasis by the apparent intention of Bill C-217 to by-pass the provinces and territories completely. The position of provincial governments and discussion on a cost-sharing formula involving the provinces are essential elements which require further consideration.
The implications of the arrangements entertained under the bill are compounded when one considers that a large majority of programs produced, or acquired by the CBC, are available

for broadcast use only and cannot be used for other purposes. In some cases the talent collective agreements under which the programs are produced do not provide for classroom use. In other cases, the non-broadcast rights may already have been licensed elsewhere. Writers, who nearly always retain copyright ownership in Canada, may not wish or be able to grant the right to use in the classroom of a program produced from their creative works.
In the case of feature films, only the broadcast rights are made available, with producers and distributors retaining postbroadcast rights. The only instance where the CBC could have post-broadcast rights would be in the case of a Canadian film with CBC production money. In drama, management contracts do a specific program but the author retains the copyright. The copyright laws in Canada specify that unless otherwise assigned, the copyright is vested with the creator.
If Bill C-217 were adopted, inevitably programmers would be under pressure to make choices that emphasize those programs for which classroom clearance is possible. The hon. member will agree, subject only to the unqualified mandate to provide the national broadcasting service defined in the act, that by far the most serious consequence for the CBC of the adoption of C-217 would be that the CBC would no longer be seen to be independent and autonomous in program matters.
The CBC is a federal agency responsible to parliament, the source of most of its funds. It has certain obligations imposed on it by the Broadcasting Act and elsewhere. An amendment of the kind proposed by Bill C-217 would give local school boards, which are under provincial jurisdiction and administration for the most part, the right to make unpredictable demands on the CBC's financial and other resources, and to alter in a major way the balanced service required of the CBC under section 3 of the act.
Serious consideration should be given to the hazards of accepting the principle of provincial influence in broadcast programming matters, even though at this time the justification appears to be popular in some parts of Canada. The bill raises more problems and questions than it solves. It fails to answer whether such a proposal has much appeal for the provinces.
Other members will speak on this important matter, but before closing may I congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) for his original idea, although I feel it cannot be agreed to at this time for the reasons I have mentioned. However, perhaps there is some room for the idea after further federal-provincial discussions and agreements have taken place.

Mr. Speaker, approximately four or five years ago I was the original seconder of the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie). As a matter of fact, we were seat mates, as well as being ex-school board trustees.
I am disappointed in the contribution made by the hon. member of Welland (Mr. Railton). He seems to have found a difficulty for every solution. I doubt very much if he will be
December 20, 1977

voted man of the year by the Welland school board after the 15-minute dissertation we have heard with respect to the duties of the CBC. According to the hon. member, the autonomy of the CBC will be destroyed if school children are allowed to see its programs before they are aired publicly. 1 never heard more rubbish in a shorter time than I heard today from the hon. member for Welland.
The CBC's autonomy is evident to everyone. The corporation produces excellent programs in an attempt to assist in the teaching of social studies. That has been the strength of this bill, and the strength of the movement toward making CBC programs available for use in the classroom.
The school boards that have gone into video tape equipment are faced with difficulties. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred to school board No. 63 which invested in VTR facilities. 1 was chairman of the Victoria school board when it invested in VTR under the assumption that the CBC was a public corporation working for the good of the Canadian public and would welcome a wider audience for its programs. I assume the corporation would welcome wider audiences for those excellent documentaries and for its excellent coverage of current affairs. The CBC was determined that no one would see its programs unless a stiff price was paid, particularly school children, which was a shocking thing to occur.
In British Columbia, the Kamloops school board set up video tape recorders in almost every school. It was able to tape every decent program produced by the CBC. The facilities were used quite freely. The effect was good. Then suddenly the school board was threatened with a lawsuit if it continued to tape off-air CBC programs for use in its schools.
This subject was raised in the House in 1974 by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. We were amazed at the quick response we received from all educators. We were promised, by the minister responsible, that he was working toward a solution. We were offered compromises, which we accepted, but they were never delivered. Nothing seemed to happen, except it was prevented from becoming the public shame it was.
A taxpayer pays for these programs to be produced by the CBC and I do not see why the taxpayer, who also pays taxes to the school district, cannot get a program by just paying once for it-why can he not pay the tax once and then his kids can watch the program? Once should be enough. There is the problem of residuals for creators of creative work. I do not know how much creative work goes into a newscast. Sometimes when I look around the House of Commons I realize there is much more creativity here than people realize, particularly in answers to questions, although there is a certain amount of creativity in questions also. I am sure that the problem of remuneration for the artists for truly artistic work could be solved.
On this side we would like this to go to committee. We want these problems to be solved and we want to come up with better solutions than we have now, which is not to leave some
Broadcasting Act
of these things which could be so useful to the education world forever in the vaults until they disintegrate perhaps a thousand years from now. It is ridiculous to think that there is something here that might be useful to schools and to our young people, but that we cannot solve the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in my participation on Bill C-217. As someone who has been a member of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts since my first election to this place in 1972, and also having the honour at present of being chairman of that committee, I am quite interested in the contents of this bill, but 1 also see a great many problems. As someone who has earned his living in the past, before becoming a member of parliament, in the field of radio and television, and specifically recalling my obligations as a member of some unions to carry out functions on television and, I think more specifically, of the Canadian Association of Radio and Television Actors, of which even newsmen had to be members, although the news people hate to admit they are actors or performers but that is part of the business, obviously 1 can find many aspects in this bill to commend to the consideration of the House.
But once you go past the good intentions there are some real difficulties which I do not think can be overlooked. To say that the CBC happens to be a Crown corporation, subsidized to a great degree by the Canadian public through federal taxes, is not to say that further down the line there will not be complications in the material that is put together to be presented. Simply to say that this material, after it has been introduced, belongs to the Canadian public and therefore should be distributed freely to school children, as this bill suggests, and that it is evil to deny them access to this material for which we as federal taxpayers have paid, I suggest, is a simplistic argument.
The hon. member who spoke before me went over some of the problems involved, but I do not think he did so with much thoroughness. Should a performer who chooses to perform for a production that is being used by the CBC waive his or her rights to residuals for repeats when the same performer, acting for any other type of media or production house or film centre in Canada, has the right to those residuals? Is it fair to say that the CBC, when it has responsibility not only to spend our money to produce programming and make it available to the Canadian public but, as some of us know in some frustration they have not done well, can come back and say they have done well and have recovered money where they can, in the interest of carrying on a viable operation, and yet try to meet their responsibility under the Broadcasting Act? I say that the cost is real within a complex society where other competitive organizations, be they other television networks or other producers of theatre, drama, or public affairs, operate under the separate rules in the business world. I suggest we cannot do that easily, as good as the idea may be.
The fact is that cost comes down to a line somewhere, and the waiving of it either puts back on the CBC an additional burden, which will be born by federal taxpayers indirectly, or

December 20, 1977
Broadcasting Act
it means that parliament or the Government of Canada would pick up the additional cost of the responsibility for a settlement of residuals rather than the CBC.
The CBC, with a budgeting range of half a billion dollars, is under great criticism, and 1 suggest we cannot easily add to its cost load and argue that we will be tough with it. In turn, when we have a massive deficit, which we now have, and we hear from the other side the arguments they put forward about restraining government spending, when we hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) ask, as he did in the question period yesterday or today, what the government is going to do to get the burden off its back as suggested by the Lambert Commission, in transferring points to the provinces whose jurisdictional responsibility is involved, I cannot see how the opposition can do what my predecessor often used to call sucking and blowing at the same time. They play a fine harmonica, but the cost of the tune must be covered by someone. In this case the cost would either directly fall on the taxpayer through the CBC or would have to be directly paid by the taxpayer through the government assuming the burden.
1 cannot see how we can do that responsibly when education is primarily the responsibility of the provinces, especially primary and secondary education.
It is a commendable proposal that the material should be made available where contracts and agreements are such that there are no additional dues owing to the people involved in the production. That is fine, but where cost factors are involved, as they are in most cases, and where the CBC has the responsibility to recover costs when it has spent money on productions, I do not think it should be the responsibility of the federal taxpayer, simply because we are not answerable for that area of jurisdiction and it distorts the whole process of our political system.

Mr. Speaker,
I do not intend to be long but I feel I have something to contribute to this debate. I know there are problems. The arguments brought forward by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) about school children and school trustees interfering in the programming of the CBC left me flabbergasted. I have not heard arguments of such vacuity put forward by the hon. member in this Chamber before, and I am quite surprised. As I see it, school teachers would be aware of the program that would be available and would apply for it, and not try to guide the CBC into a particular form of program.
I know there are problems, and we have just heard about them. The suggestion is that the matter go to the committee where these problems could be worked out. ACTRA has indicated its readiness to face these problems.
I can recall having tried when I was abroad to get a particular ballet program from the CBC. Ballet programs are most useful to use in countries where there is a language problem because ballet is a universal language; it speaks for itself. It is not a matter of having a play where you must have the translation dubbed. A ballet can be used by an embassy abroad. I tried to get one, but the CBC put up a fight and
[Mr. Fleming.)
refused, presumably on the grounds which are being advanced now that there are residuals available to the performers.
There are two solutions which I can suggest. First, I believe a school board has already agreed what a nominal fee might be. The other one is that the performers in the original performance might be given a higher fee on the understanding that some of these programs might be used in schools.
I just do not see what the government is trying to do by preventing good programs-I do not want to see bad programs in schools; there have been enough of them-which teachers could learn about and use for current affairs programs, as the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) said. Some of the historic programs we have seen on the CBC deserve to be given a much wider distribution. They could be used as a basis for discussion in social sciences classes. I just do not see why the government is trying to prevent this matter from going to committee. I would like to call for the question now so that this matter can go to committee.
It worked out in the United Kingdom.

It worked out in the
United Kingdom, and if it can work out there where unions are strong I do not see why we cannot work it out here in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite want to have their time to say something, but when someone else gets up to avail himself of the same opportunity they suggest he should be stilled and not allowed to rise. Those same members suggest that when time allocation is imposed they are being muzzled. I find this absolutely incredible.
Everything which has been said indicates that the hon. member has a good idea. I think all hon. members have indicated that the kernel of what he is saying is a good idea. No one denies that, but what has not been indicated is the direction that the CBC is already taking.
This matter was raised previously.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think this matter was initially raised in July of 1975. Since that time the CBC has made available, according to some notes I have, some 200 hours of French and English programs for circulation. New releases are being made at the rate of about 90 to 100 hours per year. A radio further use project is being developed this year with the same kinds of objectives as for TV.
The CBC's further use project is quickly gaining acceptance across Canada, and at its present rate of growth it will soon be the largest collection of Canadian programs available for use in schools. This is to say nothing with respect to the programming available through the National Film Board.
December 20, 1977

In view of the various considerations which Bill C-217 raises such as jurisdictional constraints, copyright obligations and control and responsibility of the corporation for programming, the further use program of the corporation becomes an even more logical approach to distributing CBC programs for postbroadcasting use. Already school boards and service clubs are greatly benefiting from this program free of charge. Nothwith-standing that, the letters the hon. member brings forward make no mention of this particular program, which is already in use by those same school board. However, he claims the letters support this bill.
The corporation has accepted, I submit, the responsibility of meeting the heavy demands from the public for its programs. Constrained as it is with respect to copyright and talent agreements, the corporation is nevertheless making an increasing amount of programs available for post-broadcast distribution.
That the corporation is developing a post-broadcast use program for radio attests to the seriousness and importance attributed by the CBC to the wider distribution of its programs to the public. In this respect I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) to reconsider his proposal. It seems to me that there is already a response being made by this government and by the CBC. In fact the CBC has taken it upon itself to develop this post-broadcast system.
I would not have had to introduce the bill if what you say is true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member says he would not have had to introduce the bill if what I say is true, but he fails to take into account the fact that there have been more than 200 hours of production available to school boards and the like since the hon. member brought forward his bill in 1975.
One hundred hours?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I said 200 hours. The hon. member should be listening. Two hundred hours is a fantastic amount of time. If the hon. member was being fair, where was that in his speech?
If the hon. member was being fair, he would not have said to us that the government and the CBC are denying the children of this country the opportunity to see CBC programming. In fact there is a library full of it, and it is being relied upon rather heavily.
Say that to the school boards.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not have to. The record speaks for itself. The school boards are already using it, and they are using it to a greater and greater extent. While I am speaking of that, one needs only to look at the kind of advertising that is taking place with respect to the new technology of which the hon. member speaks and what in fact is being developed.
With the new kinds of videotape cassettes and the new technology that is being used we are now getting to the point where virtually every individual in the country will have the opportunity to tape off air, and it is obviously going to be
Broadcasting Act
something in addition to the post-broadcast policy that the CBC is following. Individuals such as hon. members opposite and myself will have the opportunity to tape off air, and I wonder whether that will create problems. There have been arguments about the availability of that kind of off-air taping. It seems to me that we would be in a position to invite our closest friends to watch programs we tape on cassette machines.
Notwithstanding that, the hon. member does not seem to recognize that the CBC is moving forward and is not going to deal with the issue in the way the hon. member proposes.
To follow up on some of the comments made by my distinguished colleague, with whom the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) took such issue, I point out that the language of sub-paragraph (k) needs clarification since, among other things, there is a difference between the French and English texts. For example, the English version refers to "any broadcasting productions which are the property of the corporation" while the French text refers to "toutes production radiodiffusees appartenant a la Societe." It is not specified whether this amendment applies to all broadcasting productions including radio or just to films as it is stated in sub-paragraph (c). The expression "any broadcasting productions which are the property of the corporation" is so broad as to include any kind of radio or television broadcast, including news.
You are not married to the language.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Without wanting to cast any disrespect on the hon. member, if so little has gone into the preparation of the bill as to afford this kind of ambiguity and difficulty, I would have difficulty supporting a reference of this bill to a committee. It seems to me that perhaps we should go back to the drawing board.
Why do you introduce so many amendments to your bills?
Move an amendment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests I introduce an amendment. Perhaps that should be done, but I say that this measure should be sent back to the drawing board. It is certainly not something I would agree to referring to a committee. One has to have a kernel of something to work with in order to send it to a committee.
In addition to what I have indicated, the hon. member will no doubt agree that, if it is assumed that the amendment is intended to cover all productions by or for the CBC, there appears to be irreconcilable differences between this proposed amendment and that in sub-paragraph (c).
If we accept for the moment that these drafting problems can be overcome, the CBC must then make the assumption that in order for these amendments to have any meaning in practice the corporation will have to be aware of all the opinions of the thousands of school boards across Canada even

Hon. members opposite are having a lot of fun shouting "Question". There are several other comments I would like to make. It will only prolong the debate if they use more time by shouting "Question".
There is also the consideration that there are at least two parties to every contract. The program rights market is not regulated by price lists and is highly competitive. As soon as it became known that the CBC was required to obtain educational rights in addition to broadcast rights, the hon. member can no doubt see that the corporation would have little or no bargaining position left. The cost of this service would become prohibitive-

The hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont.

Mr. Speaker, 15 minutes is not much to formulate a foreign policy, but it is enough to express in a few words my views on some matters of concern to this House and the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to take part in this debate, as it is the first time in 17 years that we have had the opportunity in this House to look fully into the implications of a foreign policy which has considerably evolved in the last few years, and to readjust our aims if needed so that our country may be more implicated at the international level.
Mr. Speaker, the interest of Canadians in external affairs has considerably increased during the last ten years, and if one considers the participation of Canada in several major international activities, and I think particularly of Canada's decision to participate once more in the Security Council and its subsequent election to the UN Security Council, the participation of the Deputy Prime Minister as co-chairman of the fourth conference of the United Nations on trade and development, the invitation extended to the Canadian government to hold the United Nations Conference on Human Settlements in Vancouver, Canada's decision to go ahead and face the facts and thus recognize China, one of the first western nations to do so. Mr. Speaker, the ever increasing involvements of the Canadian government show the Canadian people's determina-
December 20, 1977

tion to become increasingly aware of what goes on in other countries.
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege and the honour to serve my country in the last three months as Canada's representative at the thirty-second session of the UN General Assembly, more specifically on the fifth commission, the administrative and budgetary commission. And I was in a position to become familiar with the internal operations of the United Nations, its various mechanisms and the reasons why that institution has been criticized and also why it is so necessary. This is the subject with which I should like to deal briefly this evening in the House.
Mr. Speaker, we must recognize that the UN has considerably evolved during the last 32 years. It must be kept in mind that it was created after the second world war during a difficult period following a very painful conflict, and it was created by a number of sovereign states, 57 at the time, which had interests themselves throughout the world.
Later, in subsequent years, with the fall of colonialism or at least of official colonialism, an increasing number of new nations which had gained their independence at the end of the fifties or at the beginning of the sixties joined the United Nations, and that trend is keeping up since the organization is now composed of 147 member states.
Mr. Speaker, an organization had been devised for 57 member states, with appropriate mechanisms and structures, and it is now made up of 147 member states. So, it is easy to understand why the rules of the game have changed. What was at the beginning a conflict, a potential conflict between socialist and capitalist countries, later became a conflict between colonial and decolonized countries, between developing and industrialized countries, and it is now more or less a conflict between rich and poor countries. And it is normal, Mr. Speaker, that this new majority at the United Nations, this new majority composed of poor countries, of those countries which obtained their independence and are now developing, it is normal, Mr. Speaker, that those countries stick together and often show some impatience and resentment towards richer countries which they accuse, often rightly, of being indifferent to them.
Mr. Speaker, if one is to analyse objectively what has happened to the UN in recent years, it is essential to have good understanding of the new rules of the game. Beyond the problems related to the working of the UN, with which, unfortunately, 1 will not have time to deal this evening, we have had more than an idea of those difficulties, confrontations and frictions in the working of the UN which again merely reflect the difficulties that exist between rich and poor countries, because it must be kept in mind that the United Nations are not a world government but rather a forum for discussion, a meeting place.
Therefore, we have witnessed a whole series of stances that were more or less acceptable, let us admit it, more or less applicable and often a little unrealistic, but, Mr. Speaker, they
External Affairs
didn't really have the effect that had been expected. If one understands well this esprit de corps among those poor countries, one understands better, Mr. Speaker, that some resolutions which may seem unacceptable to our country were carried with a majority. Mr. Speaker, there is a new majority in the United Nations, we have to accept that fact if the organization is to carry on, and 1, for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that the UN is a worth-while organization which must go on with its work.
1 agree.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It is certainly worth improving.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Drummond, says that it is worth improving. Any organization, and the first that comes to my mind is this very House, is worth improving. I, for one, trust that he will put all his energy into it.
And good luck!

Mr. Speaker, 1 have presented the facts in that light, it is because again this year Canada has not followed up its wish which was expressed in other forums, not to get involved in conflicts which only concerns us indirectly. Mr. Speaker, Canada is a country which is highly respected internationally in several respects. As I said earlier, this is due to the fact that our involvement in various areas, a direct involvement demonstrated by an obvious interest in various conferences.
Generally speaking, Canada has such a good image abroad that it is a sad thing that a certain emotivity should sometimes lead us to take positions that are misinterpreted by the global community and somewhat tarnish some of our efforts in other areas. This at least is the impression I got during my stay in New York.
Canada has been a leader in the area of development, and a few months ago, as all members are aware, we erased the external debt of the least developed countries. That initiative was greeted in an extraordinary way by the countries involved and by the group of underdeveloped countries as a whole. In such instances, people come forward to tell us how, marvellous it is Canada could take such a leading position. It is unfortunate that in other areas, and I think of the Middle East in particular because this is making headlines, we should take more contentious positions.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), when the time comes for this country to take a contentious position, to seriously weigh the pros and cons of both sides of the issue. In the UN we are fortunate in having a third way, open to us. I know that in Canada abstention is sometimes crucified by those who would like us to take more outstanding, extreme positions. But it is a fact at least in the United Nations forum, abstention has become an accepted way of voting that changes the name of the game. This is used on occasion by every country where, for a reason or another,
800 2 7-61 '/i

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
neither extreme reflects that country's real position in respect of the issue at hand.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that before going to New York, I myself was reluctant to chose abstention. Since that time I have seen the organization at work, and 1 have come to the realization that in some cases it is better to abstain than create enemies without reason. In the present case, and I think once more of the Middle East, there has been a tremendous opening, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself suggested, when Mr. Sadat on the one hand and Mr. Begin on the other made the necessary steps for a first and now a second meeting.
Why should we Canadians have a finger in the pie instead of letting both parties settle their conflicts, for they will have to live together peacefully? Once again I urge the Canadian government to change its emotional approach and not to play partisan politics as it has been the case many times in the past when time came to appreciate the situation.
As I do not want to be long, Mr. Speaker, and my time is running short, I will take a few minutes to deal with the francophone Africa issue. A few days ago in Abidjan the Agency for Cultural and Technical Co-operation concluded its meetings. Unfortunately, institutional conflicts between France and the Quebec and Canadian delegations prevented the Agency for Cultural and Technical Co-operation from making a head start toward fulfilling the aims which were at the base of its creation, that is multilateral co-operation between Francophone countries.
Mr. Speaker, I regret that those poor countries in Africa or elsewhere have to wait for any kind of help from rich and industrialized country, and in this case they had a tool they could have used to help those countries fulfill their aspirations and develop themselves. I regret that once again conflicts- and I repeat, institutional conflicts-stood in the way of progress. I cannot help blaming the French government, however mildly, for its somewhat unflexible position towards multilateral co-operation. All of us know that after the colonization, France created special relations with those countries bilateral relations, and I suppose it does no want other Francophone countries such as Canada to share that co-operation with Francophone nations. For our part, we are wrong sometimes, we are concentrating too much on domestic issues and we do not like to see a full-fledged Quebec delegation attending those international meetings.
Mr. Speaker, let us forget our little domestic problems until the next conference, let us have bilateral relations with France in order to settle those issues so that once and for all co-operation between Francophone countries might work, that we might have, and 1 put them between quotes because they are banned words, a "Francophone Commonwealth".

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be participating in this debate, not the first foreign affairs debate in 17 years. It is quite wrong to suggest that;
[Mr. Lachance.)
there have been a larger number prompted by the opposition over that period of time.
I want to congratulate the minister for the high tone he took in leading off the debate. I say to him now, as I said to him in the committee not long ago, that we are proud of him as an eloquent and articulate spokesman for our country abroad. On occasion we do not agree with him, but we admire the way he expresses himself. His speech the other day was a credit to him, to his country, and to the department. 1 was very proud of the whole tone of the debate. Almost without exception, no one descended into party politics at any time. Our leader, who has proven himself knowledgeable on national issues, demonstrated a dimension of statesmanship the other day, showing he has a grasp of international issues which bodes well for the potential prime minister of this country.
Hear, hear!

I was particularly pleased at his reference to the late L. B. Pearson. There never was a finer or nobler Canadian. I admired what my leader had to say about the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), a leading expert in the study of aid and development who proved himself, as he always does, a most competent, perceptive, and sensitive statesman.
The Middle East has been a major concern of mine for many years, Mr. Speaker, but the subject will not form a major portion of my truncated speech. Like all people of good will who believe that love is better than hate and peace better than war, I rejoiced at the recent meeting in that ancient and beautiful city which our old hymn describes as "Jerusalem the Golden". I predict that President Sadat will become the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize and I hope nobody will think me anti-American if I say that it is an even greater designation than being named Time magazine's "Man of the Year." But we must not allow our yearnings or our responses to the theatre and the drama of the Jerusalem meeting to blind our perception of some sombre truths. Psalm 85 in the Presbyterians' beloved Old Testament contains a pregnant message "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."
No matter how amiable are the relations or the accords between Prime Minister Begin and President Sadat, there will be no lasting or worthy peace in the Middle East which forgets the suffering or ignores the rights of the chief victims of the Middle East situation, the Palestinians. It was not a good omen when the Israeli delegate to the Cairo conference the other day refused to participate in the presence of an empty chair which had been designated for the PLO, and called for the hauling down of the PLO flag outside the building. Whether we like it or not, the PLO is the most widely supported Palestinian organization at this time.
Until the Palestinians have a state of their own they will not be able to go through the process of formally selecting a government. And not all members of the PLO are terrorists, as we are so often told they are by the biased media. President Sadat aired the case for the Palestinians well in the Knesset.

Let us hope it will not be lost in any bilateral discussions which take place.
The return of Sinai to Egypt and a separate peace between that country and Israel will not solve nor settle the Middle East crisis. There is a danger in rushing some of these things too fast. The American word "momentum" has been used in connection with the operation: it is being said we must maintain the momentum. We should be less interested in momentum, I believe, Sir, than we should be interested in peace.
Other states must be involved. I refer to Syria, whose commitment to the suffering Palestinians has been both powerful and painful, and to Jordan, whose moderation and wisdom are and always were a hopeful and helpful element. I congratulate His Majesty the King on the celebration of his twenty-fifth anniversary of his reign, as we did the Queen of our own country.
Hear, hear!

Saudi Arabia is a thoroughly dependable ally for peace and good will. There is long suffering Lebanon and, most of all, the Palestinians. These people must be in the equation if a successful formula is to be worked out. As for our role in connection with a recent UN resolution, I made clear my view on that at the committee meeting and 1 shall not repeat it tonight. The hon. gentleman who spoke before me talked about the use of abstention. On that resolution, 32-20, instead of voting with El Salvador, the United States and Israel against everybody else, it would have been wise to have abstained. I regret profoundly that we did not do so.
When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) was in my party I hardly ever agreed with him. Quite often at national meetings the party supported his view rather than mine, which leads me to believe that at times parties, like individuals, deserve what they get. In the instance of the boycott 1 am more inclined to be with him in his realism than with certain other people. The main issue is surely not the Arab boycott in its primary, secondary and tertiary elements. The main thing is to settle the reason for the boycott, namely, the insistent state of war. That is why there is a boycott. It is because these states are technically still at war. Can you imagine Winston Churchill saying "In war we can use only certain kinds of boycott"? He would use them all, of course. The settlement of the issue is of the essence.
I think we could do more in the Middle East if we were more objective. I heard Professor Peyton Lyon on radio this morning saying we had lost our capacity there because we are regarded as being too pro-Israel. I should like to see the day when we could regain true objectivity. It is conceivable that the nations may not v ant to go to Geneva for renewal of the conference. They cer:?inly would not wish to go to Washington because a meeting there would be held under the wing of a great power. I would like to see Canada in a position to invite all the participants to come to Ottawa. We are peacekeepers. We are proud of this role. We had a great tradition in the days of Mr. Pearson when there was a crucial, troubled time in the Middle East and Canada was in the forefront. Perhaps an
External Affairs
objective Canada, unbiased, might be the scene of a renewed conference of Middle East states.
I was interested in what the minister had to say about South Africa. I am being careful not to be hostile, but I am a little troubled. I think it is sometimes dangerous to be too brittle in one's attitude toward these matters. I wonder if I were allowed a question a day by Mr. Speaker and if every day I brought up to the minister cases of a country in which human rights were being grossly violated, and asked if we were going to sever trade relations with it, how many days it would take and how much international trade we would have left. This is a very serious situation. If the minister wishes to read Amnesty International he will find there are a great many countries involved. But more serious than that and something which troubles me is that perhaps outside criticism makes it more difficult for the moderates within South Africa.
There are men of good will inside South Africa. There are moderates there, and the ganging up of the outside world has the inevitable result of making the extremists more popular in that country. That is a great danger with this sort of thing. We want to give room to the moderate men, to people of good will. There have been some forward steps taken in South Africa but no one ever mentions them. Their system, of course, is iniquitous, but do you bring improvements to the people one wants to help most by ringing them round with a circle of hostile criticism?
I am always a little ill at ease when I hear these criticisms of the majority at the United Nations. I am old enough to remember when majorities in the United Nations General Assembly were good things because they were nearly always controlled by the United States and they were nearly always from Latin America. So it was a great thing to be in the majority. I remember all the work which was done to bring that majority into play to create the State of Israel. But now majorities are considered bad. It is unwise for Canadians to get into that act as to whether a little state is as important as a big one. Does Canada say that being a small province is less valuable than being a big one? There are troubles when one gets into that seeming condescension of criticizing countries which are both small and non-white.
It is strange that there are certain occasions when the majority is damned, but when it comes to Africa we justify our actions by indicating that we are with the majority. An inconsistency such as that troubles me. If I had more time I would wax eloquently and logically as to where that will lead us.

Mr. Speaker, 1 intended to deal with a number of subjects, but since 1 am limited to 1 5 minutes 1 will avoid that temptation. 1 should like to talk about the situation in the Middle East. I talk about that subject not only because it is one of the most important up front subjects in international affairs today, but because I am a Jew and a Zionist.
For the past 35 years that the State of Israel has been in existence, it has been pleasing to note how strongly Canadians support it and its right to existence. That state is supported by Canadians for a number of important reasons. It is recognized that Israel is the historic homeland of Jewish people because they have a special historic claim on it, and also because Jews have been present there for thousands of years. An hon. member opposite suggested that it was a Palestinian state from which the Palestinians had been ejected, which is not true. It was as much a Jewish state as it was a Palestinian state at any time during the recent past. Strong colonies of Jews lived in Israel during the period when it was a trustee territory and

during the period when it was a colony. Thus, it is not a Palestinian state.
Canadians support Israel as well because they remember the holocaust and the near destruction of the Jewish people during the Second World War. No one can view that situation without seeing some sense of justice in the result achieved by the Jews in being able to re-establish the Jewish homeland in some small corner of the world. Canadians recognize and appreciate that Israel is a solid democracy, at a time when democratic states are few in number, particularly in the Near East. Israel is a democracy. It shares many institutions with Canada. It has our admiration and respect for that reason.
Israel is watched with interest and respect because of the social experiments which take place there. Even Canada, with its longer history and its vastly different situation economically, socially, and politically, has learned things from the small state of Israel and its willingness to experiment.
Finally the courage of the state of Israel, surrounded as it has been since its formation by hostile neighbours, and the courageous manner in which Israel has conducted itself and protected itself, are respected and admired by Canadians.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) indicated that the Arab boycott would end when there was peace in the Middle East. There will be peace in the Middle East when Israel's right to survive is accepted by her neighbours. Israel's enemies would like to argue that peace is being held up because of occupied territory. I remind the House that Israel was facing hostilities and enemies when there was no occupied territory. How can it be argued that it is the occupied territory which is standing in the way of peace? Before there was occupied territory, there was war against the state of Israel. The Palestinian question is raised as a reason why there will not be peace in the Middle East. Before there were any Palestinian refugees, there was war against the state of Israel. Thus it is not the Palestinians and their legitimate aspirations to be settled and cease to be refugees-that is not a fundamental cause of the problem.
Also it is argued that there should be a Palestinian state, and if a Palestinian state were established on the occupied west bank then there would be peace in the Middle East. This has been put forward as an impediment to peace. The west bank belongs to the Arab side. It belonged to them before 1967. If the Palestinians wanted a homeland on the west bank, it could have been established before Israel occupied the territory, before the last two wars were necessary.
None of these alleged problems is the reason for the hostility. The survival of the state of Israel is the issue. The Palestine Liberation Organization claims to represent Palestinians, and if it were willing to acknowledge the right of the state of Israel to survival then there would be peace in the Middle East. As well as the hon. member for Hillsborough, I yearn for peace; but also I should like to make it clear that there could be peace in the Middle East and there could be negotiations with the Palestinians if only the PLO and Israel's other neighbours were prepared to recognize Israel's right to exist. It is because of that, I think, that the Canadian people stand so strongly at
December 20, 1977

the side of Israel and, I am pleased to say, the Government of Canada does so as well. Israel is not referred to by her neighbours as the state of Israel but rather as the Zionist entity. There is an unwillingness after 30 odd years to grant to the state of Israel its designation. But things are changing rapidly.
The Middle East stands today at a crucial crossroad hovering between movement toward peace and movement toward war. The major countries involved in determining the future of the region-Egypt, Jordan and Israel-are showing important signs of moderation and a willingness to negotiate. Other Arab countries-Syria, Iraq, Libya, Algeria, South Yemen-are consolidating an extremist, destructive, negative stance that calls for the destruction of Israel and the continuation of conflict and warfare. At the recent Tripoli conference these latter states, together with the Palestine Liberation Organization, all signed a communique attacking Egypt for its peace initiatives and refusing to do anything that would help bring about peace in the region. On the contrary, those states and the PLO called for the destruction of the "Zionist entity", and, in the words of U.S. President Carter, have thus provided a totally negative response to all the recent positive developments.
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, a major behind-the-scenes power broker, has kept its views quietly to itself; however, it is generally believed that King Khaled and his advisers support the Egyptian initiative and seek its success. I wish only that the hon. member for Hillsborough would do the same.
Israel has always sought peace with its Arab neighbours, and its prime ministers have always been willing and eager to go anywhere in the world to discuss peace. Every Israeli prime minister has publicly declared his willingness to go to any Arab capital to discuss peace. Thus it did not surprise anyone when Prime Minister Begin made the same offer made by President Sadat only six months earlier. The Egyptian leader stunned the world with his announcement because it represented a major shift in the stance of the major Arab country-a shift from an emphasis on war to one on peace.
At the present time Egypt and Israel are negotiating directly, in a face-to-face manner, at the Cairo conference. In and of itself this represents a vindication, even an initial triumph, of the position taken by the Canadian government under successive secretaries of state for external affairs-and that position was embodied in the texts of UN Security Council resolution 338 of 1973, which incorporated UN Security Council resolution 242 of 1967-a resolution in whose development Canada played a major role. That position to which I refer is the call for direct negotiations between the parties as the only viable and potentially successful form of such talks. The Canadian government has repeatedly said that the breakthroughs that are required would only develop via such a framework, and it may in some way be due to our reiteration of this position that the Egyptian government has come around and accepted this
External Affairs
perspective-one, I might add, that Israel has always shared with our government.
In the present context a major destructive element is played by the United Nations. I do not agree with the hon. member of Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) that the right thing to do is to go along with the majority, whatever that majority might want. I would rather agree with the hon. member for Hillsborough that the policy of following the majority for its own sake can only lead to difficulty when the majority takes a swing in a different direction at some subsequent time.
The right thing to do in foreign policy, and in particular in our voting at the United Nations, is to try to take positions on resolutions which correspond with the fundamental moral stance of the Canadian people. I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) that our foreign policy in this country is bi-partisan. It generally happens that the Canadian people know their mind on major foreign issues. I think, in connection with the issue of the Middle East, that it would be indefensible for this government to come forward with a policy of abstaining or of voting with the majority for its own sake. No one expects or would want the government to do that.
I am very pleased that of late our delegation has taken important and strong stances on a number of UN votes, stances of which all Canadians should be proud. In an era when courage of convictions seems to come very cheap and where company in UN votes is often sought at too high a price, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) took a strong and clear position in voting together with Israel, El Salvador, and the United States against a blatantly biased resolution on the situation in the Middle East. This was a resolution which would undermine resolution 242 which has been responsible, I would argue, for laying a foundation upon which Egypt and Israel could meet.
That resolution completely prejudged the outcome of the Middle East negotiations and called for complete Israeli withdrawal from all occupied territory as well as for PLO participation in the peace process. It condemned the continuation of the occupation by Israel, ignoring the basic reason for that continued occupation, the reason I referred to at the outset, the Arab refusal to discuss peace. This is all to the good. Now would certainly have been the wrong time to introduce gratuitous, biased resolutions that would have Israel surrender everything and receive nothing in return. The minister was correct in being irritated by these senseless resolutions, and so will all concerned and aware Canadians. Similarly, in recent votes on even more vicious resolutions on the Palestine question, resolutions that called for the destruction of Israel, Canada stood firm and opposed their passage.

Mr. Speaker, I am all the more happy to take part in this debate that we seldom have the opportunity in this House to discuss our foreign policy. At the same time, I regret that the House generally devotes so little time to the discussion of matters concerning foreign

affairs. In doing so Mr. Speaker, we unfortunately give support to the suggestion that among the many government activities, foreign affairs is somehow a marginal area to which attention is called simply in case of parliamentary missions abroad. For many people foreign policy can only be of continuing interest for a few star gazers who cannot see real problems which confront a politician.
Mr. Speaker, is view of this unfortunately widespread attitude in political circles, it is no wonder that Canadians in general see very little importance in the foreign policy of their country. 1 believe that the House should set an example and bear witness to the vital nature of our international relations by once a year setting aside at least two or three days to debate the foreign policy of the government.
Mr. Speaker, that a government should establish realtions with as many countries as possible or participate in the activities of various international institutions, is certainly not a luxury. On the contrary, it is the government's duty to contribute to the establishment of harmonious relations between all countries of the world and, hence, to safeguard world peace, without which everything is meaningless because, Mr. Speaker, what good would it be to eradicate unemployment in this country, to stabilize prices, to ensure material security for all Canadians or to make the country more united if we were to wake up tomorrow in a world faced with a nuclear holocaust? We should not kid ourselves, if a major world war should break out, it would be extremely difficult not to use the ultimate weapon.
Mr. Speaker, there is a great number of questions relating to international relations that have direct impact upon Canadians' day-to-day lives, but none can evidently match disarmament in importance. Since the end of World War II, the destructive capacity of nuclear weapons has steadily increased, both in quantity and quality. Moreover, the risk of proliferation of these weapons is greater than ever. We also see a disturbing proliferation and an ever greater degree of sophistication of conventional weapons. In short, although eight international multilateral agreements have been concluded since I960 and although a dozen other bilateral agreements between Soviet Union and the United States have also been signed, the arms race is nevertheless gaining momentum. The world military expenditure, established in 1960 at $100 billion annually, have escalated to $400 billion a year, a situation all the more revolting and absurd that there are so many developing countries taking part in this foolish race, at the expense of the well-being of their own people.
Furthermore when we consider that the two superpowers actually have the military capability to kill over 100 billion human beings and that 40 per cent of all research and development expenditures in the world are used for military purposes, one question comes to mind: is man the reasonable animal described by ancient philosophers? Mr. Speaker, it is rather discouraging to see that the pace at which the various ongoing negotiations are progressing is such that it cannot match the pace of the frightening progress made by military technology.
