According to experts, the world is about to konw a real explosion, a real revolution I should say as far as new nuclear and conventional weapons are concerned and this, in a context where nuclear proliferation and terrorism are also becoming more and more threatening. Mr. Speaker, having said this, the nations of the world should put a good deal of hope in the special session of the general assembly of the United Nations on disarmament which is to be held next spring. As sponsor of the resolution asking for this special session, Canada will have to bring an original and positive contribution.
Having renounced a long time ago all desire to belong to the nuclear club, although it had the capability, our country enjoys in this area a sort of moral authority which permits it to demonstrate a leadership which unfortunately escaped it some 15 years ago, except of course in the area of nuclear arm non-proliferation, for it is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that Canada was one of the first countries to decide last year to export its nuclear technology only to countries which agreed to submit their whole nuclear programs to international controls.
Mr, Speaker, as it is important for Canadian parliamentarians to contribute to the drafting of the policy which the Canadian delegation will support during this special session of the General Assembly of the United Nations, I suggested recently the setting up of a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, a subcommittee which would hear expert opinions on the disarmament issue and report to the House on the position Canada should adopt before the United Nations on this occasion. Therefore I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will realize the importance of such an initiative and that the House will authorize without any further delay the establishment of this subcommittee which already has the approval of many of my colleagues from both sides of the House, including the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence-
I support this idea wholeheartedly.

who is telling us that he supports this idea wholeheartedly.
Mr. Speaker, among the other issues that might directly affect the life and welfare of Canadians, one is certainly the Middle East issue. Talking about this, we must remember how concerned all Canadians were at the time of the last conflict between Israel and the Arabs in the fall of 1973. In this respect, it is to be hoped that in the future our country will never again be in such an embarrassing position and that its neutrality in this conflict will be so obvious that, should the conflict flare up again, which of course I and all others hope would not happen, we will not have to be afraid of finding ourselves cut off from our oil supplies.
It is always touchy, Mr. Speaker, to deal with a matter so fraught with emotions and involving a country with which many Canadians have special ties and of which they can rightfully be proud. Moreover, special care and caution must be exercised in dealing with this matter since for the first time
December 20, 1977

peace does not seem to be out of reach any more in the Middle East.
Israel being the only truly democratic state in the Middle East, it is only natural that Canadians in general feel quite sympathetic toward it. However, it is also quite natural that occasionally Canada has to show amicable disagreement over certain policies of that state. Indeed, it is fundamental that the Canadian policy on the situation in the Middle East be first dictated by the interests of Canada and by a desire to help establish peace in the world. I am happy to note that over the years the Canadian policy is more and more characterized by objectiveness and neutrality, but unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it still happens that positions endorsed by the United Nations general assembly seem to spring from considerations that have very little to do with the contents of the resolutions we have to decide upon.
There is now a lingering hope of peace in the Middle East, but we must not entertain any illusions, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Hillsborough(Mr. Macquarrie). Whileit is important that the fundamental right of the state of Israel to exist within safe borders be recognized, it is also important to give satisfaction to the legitimate interests of Palestinians and to obtain their full involvement in any negotiations concerning their future as a community. Any hope of a final and definitive solution of the Middle East issue will be an illusion unless it is decided to establish a homeland or some territorial framework enabling Palestinians to assert themselves politically.
1 think it is up to the Palestinians themselves to decide whether their homeland should have complete political autonomy or whether it should be part of a larger political entity of a federal or confederal nature. Mr. Speaker, I was extremely pleased to learn about the Government of Canada's new policy toward South Africa and its policy of apartheid. I want to congratulate the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs who has been responsible for those major changes in our foreign policy. 1 always believe that it was not enough to denounce racism, but that it was also necessary to express in a tangible way our disgust at any policy denying human dignity, even though certain sacrifices had to be made. The steps announced yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs are a very appropriate extension of the policy statements which up to now Canada, with a few exceptions, had found satisfactory and I am sure the government will have the support of a majority of Canadians in the implementation of those measures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to deal briefly with a matter about which I feel very strongly, the human rights issue. Canada, in due time, did condemn countries like Chile which are guilty of human rights violations, more particularly at the UN General Assembly. I am surprised, however, that international financial institutions which had somehow starved President Allende's leftist regime, should show new generosity since the coming to power of the military junta of the bloodthirsty dictator Pinochet and that Canada's representatives
External Affairs
within those international institutions should support such a position. For example, 1 would mention that the World Bank withheld any economic assistance to Chile in the years 1971, 1972 and 1973, but that country received $13, $20 and $33 million from the World Bank in 1974, 1975 and 1976. The Inter-American Development Bank provided Chile with $158 million worth of economic assistance in the years 1974 and 1975 when that assistance had only reached $7 million in 1972 and 1973. I do not agree that we should not make moral judgments and that economic decisions should only be made based on the credit worthiness of the countries involved. I hope in that respect that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will soon be able to have a surprise for this House as beautiful as the magnificent Christmas present he offered us yesterday in the form of our policy toward South Africa.

Mr. Speaker, there are a couple of good things about being on the backbenches-I will start with the first one-especially if you have been on the backbenches for quite a while because you get a feeling of deja vu-of having been through this thing before.
1 recall in 1965 when Walter Gordon, a great and good man, was minister of finance. He spoke to some of us privately about what he was going to do with Time and Reader's Digest. He said they were not going to get away with things. But somehow or other he was not able to persuade his cabinet colleagues of the wisdom of that policy and when he introduced legislation regarding magazines, Time and Reader's Digest were exempted. Since he could not take care of that kind of situation I would not have minded if he had left it at that, but he was not satisfied to do so. He dragged out poor Lord Thomson and made him the butt of everything that was evil in the publishing industry.
I feel tonight as I did then. I never thought I would rise to come to the defence of Lord Thomson, nor did 1 think 1 would ever rise to come to the defence of South Africa. The same kind of hypocrisy, the same kind of cheap morality, and the same kind of double standard, however, have been foisted on this House not only by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) but by spokesmen of this side of the House.
When we look around the world and see the kind of evil that is manifest in country after country, to single out South Africa as the object of our new found morality is too much. It is just too much. It shows how much a tool this country has become of those forces in the United Nations. Foreign policy is not made on Sussex Street any more; foreign policy is made in New York on behalf of the United Nations, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, like Walter Gordon, a great and good man privately, now becomes a kind of mouthpiece.
There was a time when 1 would have been proud, as an early supporter of the United Nations and of the League of Nations before it, to have found myself in harmony with the United Nations and its resolutions, but not any more. I cannot feel that way when I see the kind of double standards that exist in the United Nations. Things used to be simple for us reformers.

When I think of the atrocities that have been recorded in Chile, and consider the cheap shot we have taken at South Africa-it is a cheap shot. After all, what harm is it going to do South Africa? Withdraw our ambassador then. Do to Chile what is being done to South Africa. I have nothing against morality if the minister wants to be moral, but this is typical. I want to know the rationale for the sudden burst of this nice nellyism of ours. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) at least is consistent. He does business with everybody and says that as far as morality is concerned we will just close our eyes and not worry about it. That, at least, is consistent. I may not agree with it but I can understand it.
When the Prime Minister rose during question period today and tried to explain to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) how he makes the distinction regarding South Africa so that South Africa is singled out, the Prime Minister in his own words said, "I know murder, mayhem and all the rest is going on in other countries, but we do it to South Africa because South Africa has technically, legally, constitutionally, apartheid in its system." He is like Professor Higgins when he talked about the French-they really don't care what they do, just how they pronounce it. The fact that people are being murdered in Chile does not count because it is not in their constitution to murder people in prison. In South Africa it counts. That is really what I find so offensive. If we are going to tackle this let us do it with an even hand. There is an argument to be made for morality. I do not underestimate morality but why do things in this particular way? We can only be suspicious of this easy, cheap way of getting off by showing the moral superiority of the government.
The minister knows, and examples have been brought to his attention, of Canadian companies that are being blacklisted and blackmailed in the Middle East. Yet there has not been a word of public condemnation of this kind of action. I can understand them not wanting to publish it. I am reluctant even to raise the question because the people involved are so frightened. They have reason to be frightened. They can be made or broken by this kind of black-list, yet the government on whom they depend and rely does not have the courage to stand on their behalf and take some action.
If I use strong language like cowardice, it is because I do not know what other language to use to describe what is going on. I listened to this debate meander all over the place with everybody saying nice things. It is an advantage of a backbencher that you do not have to be nice and you do not have to say nice things. In fact, things are neither nice nor clear. The government can always say it is only a backbencher sounding off.
I suspect that some of the sentiments I am echoing probably more closely reflect the way people in this country feel that the noble sentiments of the minister, certainly the decision that he is going to make an example of South Africa. One can only come to the conclusion that the example is purely political in scope.

speechtext: Shame! Small! Cheap!
The minister can say that if he wishes. I can understand that he feels very strongly about it.

speechtext: You certainly have.

As the minister knows, I am not normally in this kind of mood. However, I do not feel proud of the kind of

December 20, 1977

program and the kind of foreign affairs policy that has been presented to this House in the last couple of days. 1 do not see the kind of distinction that the minister and his department make on this issue.
There are others who wish to speak who feel as strongly as 1 feel about this issue. However, I did want to raise it tonight, even though the language is considerably in excess of the language I usually use. I want to say that the government is wrong, it is in an indefensible position and is not being morally courageous and morally correct in what it is doing.

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to compliment the minister on his delivery yesterday. Through an hour and a half of that golden voice I was almost led to believe that he was part of the heavenly chorus of this season of the year and we had truly peace on earth. However, under the glittering tinsel of the golden voice was a pretty shabby tree that had been tinselled up for the occasion. There was no smell of frankincense or myrrh about it, but the reek of a double standard.
1 was driven to look at the New York speech of the minister.
I was particularly struck by the opening there where he had the pleasure of welcoming two new members to the assembly, the Republic of Djibouti and the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. My mind went back about two and a half years ago when something called the Republic of South Vietnam was set up and recognized by this government with indecent haste. It disappeared as one of the most ephemeral governments ever to exist on the face of the earth, now incorporated into the Socialist Republic; no vote of the people, no majority rule, no one man one vote there. No mention of the boat people who find it necessary to risk their lives in open boats to reach Australia or some other sanctuary and are doing that at the cost of enormous suffering.
I am sure he got through that welcome without for a moment losing his smile, and his crash course in diplomacy has provided him with that.
As we prepared for this debate, 1 noticed that the Ottawa Citizen came out with a major article entitled "Canada's Shiny Image Tarnished at U.N." written by Azhar Ali Khan. As usual it lists the standard litany of left wing causes that we apparently backed in past years and ones that would bring the praise of the entire world for doing so. 1 have not time to list them all tonight, but they are there.
It also takes after the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). Here is one place 1 do not agree with them. I would like to praise the minister at this time for at least bringing a breath of fresh air into the United Nations General Assembly.
In spite of that, the author of the article says it was a scathing attack and an unexpected tirade. He even said it was reminiscent of former U.S. ambassador Patrick Moynihan. That did make me smile a little. Certainly compared to the polished harpoons of Moynihan with their explosive charges, it was bit of squid jigging that went on in the United Nations that afternoon.
External Affairs
The important thing is that, even as mild and meek as the minister's reprimands were at the United Nations, they landed on him. He was landed on with enormous weight as though he had done irreparable damage to the cause of Canada by pointing out that those carefully drafted resolutions on Israel and South Africa were a waste of time, repetitive, and bringing the assembly into disrepute.
The hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) picked up this enormous urge of the press and of some people that we should always be popular at the United Nations. I am glad the minister found the courage to vote and to join a handful of countries; Canada, the United States, Israel and El Salvador. It was about time that we ceased the pattern of abstention on outrageous resolutions before the United Nations. The problem with the continual abstention is that it adds to the fiction that there is a moral world community. We have heard that expression. The minister uses it himself. It is as if there was a commonality of interest displayed at the United Nations with which we can safely go along almost all of the time when no such thing exists.
There is no peace in this world and a great danger. When Moynihan said we were assailed, meaning the United States, but it would apply to us, because we were democracies and because we were right it is true. That is the enemy totalitarian forces on either side, be they communist or be they fascist on the other side, and they exist in this world. The kind of democracy we have in this country is open to attack at all times.
I wonder if we are as vigilantly on guard against extraterritoriality when the threat is from Arab states as we were when it was from Americans and we wanted to trade with Cuba. That, of course, is one of the left wing issues that is held up as a marvellous high point in Canadian external affairs. Of course nothing is said after the passage of time about what has grown out of that and the position of Cuba in the world today.
I was struck by lines in the minister's speech to the effect that this is the thirty-third Christmas without a global conflict. Again one was almost lulled into the thought that peace had arrived. However, there are wars going on in this world. They are dirty and miserable wars. There is one in Ethiopia versus Somalia, and versus Eritrea and goodness knows who all else. It brings back haunting memories to one such as myself who is old enough to remember that earlier war in Ethiopia that the world tried to ignore when Mussolini's Italy invaded it. Now that country is in agony again. Who is there to complain now? Who can name the dead? Who can number them, either in Addis Abbaba or elsewhere? The conscience of the world is less bothered. I know that this country is less concerned about Ethiopia now than it was in 1935 at its most isolationist stage.
There is a war going on in Morocco and Mauritania. Who will name the dead there? Who will number them? We probably would not have heard about it at all had the French apparently not strayed into that the other day. It suddenly became newsworthy once it was not confined only to African countries.
80027-62Vi

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
There is another war going on in Angola. There we have some names and we can bring them to the attention of this House. Let me quote Betty Bridgman, repatriated missionary from Angola. She said this:
On June 1 we rose to find Cuban and government soldiers had invaded the hospital and a neighboring village. They rounded up all the mem of every age and marched half of them away. Then they lined them up and shot and killed 16, leaving their bodies for their families to find the next day. One of those killed was Frederico Kacuku, one of our senior nurses, a gentle and peaceloving man, who had spent his life relieving the suffering of others. Another was Eduardo Morim, the carpenter who made artificial limbs for the amputees at the hospital. One old man was nearly 80, and he was killed along with his son who left a family of small children.
I know that Steve Biko is mourned, and rightly so because of his youth and ability and because of the loss of a person who might have made a difference in South Africa. But who will mourn Jonas Zavimbi when and if he is hunted down in Angola and destroyed? He was a leader who grew out of the work of this country in that land but was abandoned by the western world when Cuba moved in. I still wonder what it is about that state that permits it to supply mercenaries for the rest of the world without criticism on the world scene.
I wonder how the minister could have got through that section of his speech on South Africa yesterday knowing that our handling of native affairs in this land has been almost an unmitigated disaster from beginning to end. It seems to me that one of the qualifications for any Secretary of State for External Affairs in this country is that he first serve a year in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development as minister. If he had to wrestle week in and week out with the problems of that department, I do not believe he would be able to speak as sanctimoniously as the minister did yesterday.
1 was very much concerned to hear the minister promise peacekeeping forces. He said that if he thought conditions and the time were ripe he would send them to Rhodesia, and that the same was true with Namibia. This reminds me of a warning from the Times of London, whose reporter filed his story from Johannesburg. Speaking of South West Africa he has this to say:
Strategists believe that the Ovambo homeland which faces the border could be overrun in 48 hours if the South African army pulled out.
I do not believe that this nation knows what is being promised on our behalf, as we seem willing and prepared to move into situations about which we know little, where the danger is enormous and where the results could divide this nation. It seems to me it was a former prime minister, Mr. Meighen, who made the mistake of saying "Ready, aye ready" many years ago when intervening in a dispute a long way from here. It is startling to find a minister of this government, this late in the day, saying virtually the same thing, that he is ready to become involved in a situation which can bring no good to this country nor to South West Africa. No encouragement should be given the United Nations to continue its rather insane adventure in that part of the world.
Trade measures were mentioned. It is just unbelievable that the trade representatives in Johannesburg and Pretoria are to

be withdrawn when there has been a large mission from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce sent to Indonesia, including a representative of the Export Development Bank, particularly in view of the Amnesty International report. Amnesty International has had tough things to say about South Africa. It has drawn the attention of the world to that country for many years. However, speaking of Indonesia, Amnesty has this to say:
The unchanging pattern of political imprisonment in Indonesia presents the gravest challenge to the concept of international responsibility for human rights.
They put it beyond South Africa.
In no other country of the world are so many political prisoners held without trial for so many years as in the Republic of Indonesia.
That is but one excerpt from a lengthy report. Our representatives have just spent five days in that country discussing Canada's participation in a billion dollar project, a coal mining operation, I am sure the announcement will come early in the new year-yet we have the nerve-to withdraw our representatives from South Africa. Again one wonders where is the logic in the approach we are taking.
Then again today during the question period there was the warning of continued co-operation with and loans to Cuba. Why should we finance that government so long as it is maintaining its forces in Angola? The same reporter in the United Church Observer says that her impression is that there is now more oppression than ever there was under the Portuguese in their day. I cannot believe that we can still be engaged in financing Cuba in any operation there.
There is a terrible selectivity to the approach of this government to external affairs. I find it remarkable that there is no mention in this report of the return of parliamentary democracy under a constitutional monarchy to Spain. There is a miracle of the modern world-that that nation could go from the dictatorship of Francisco Franco to a parliamentary democracy modelled much like ours without any intervening civil war. Surely our government could have taken note of that at the first opportunity, because it serves as a reminder to us that the system we have is not all that bad. I suspect one of the reasons it is not mentioned, and one of the reasons why an earlier motion of mine was turned back by that side of the House, is that it indicates the usefulness and importance of the constitutional monarchy in a country which has deep and important divisions.
Although I find some things to praise in the minister's speech I hope the minister will take a more realistic attitude in the United Nations, in spite of the evils of apartheid. We are trading with nations we treat as partners. We are welcome there and we welcome them and trade with them. We know that their prisons are crowded with political prisoners, this happens all over the world. But why should we single out just one or two nations? The problem with the United Nations is that their resolutions now single out only two nations, Israel and South Africa, and the fiction is created, aided and abetted by this government, that somehow the world community as a moral force is united in its condemnation of those two nations.
I do not believe that we should put ourselves in the position of
December 20, 1977

continuing to contribute to that sort of nonsense. Until such time as we have solved the problems in this country-
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity of debating, along with other members of the House, Canada's stand on various international relations and to hear so many members speak on these matters with such enthusiasm and interest. It is regrettable that we cannot have such debates more frequently, as we do not have the forum that we have here in the House of Commons in the Standing Committee on National Defence and External Affairs. However, I hope things will improve in the future.
This debate on Canada's international relations is very timely. It comes not one day too soon as we follow with amazement the swift pace of the historic negotiations between Israel and Egypt in this last month of 1977 as well as the progress of another history-making meeting which is now taking place in Belgrade which is reviewing the implementation of the commitments contained in the Helsinki Final Act and the conclusion of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
In saying this I do not discount the importance of the war between Ethiopia and Somalia, as well as other wars and upheavals in many parts of Africa which are heating up each passing day. We must not forget the people who have lost their lives in these wars and upheavals and we must not fail to speak out, as these tragedies are tremendous ones. Canada, as a member of NATO and the Commonwealth, has a particular interest and concern in these grave developments.
Economics dominated the international scene last year. The economic situation has important implications for Canada whose growth depends a great deal on international trade and co-operation. It is to the credit of the federal government that we are making great efforts to work for an orderly and equitable evolution of the international economic system, for example, by participating in the Conference of International Economic Co-operation and expanding its development assistance program. The possibility of an interdependent world order based on peaceful relations and justice depends upon collective action in a world which inexorably is becoming smaller, more populated and increasingly industrialized.
We must, however, face hard facts and come to terms with the real world. The explosion of east-west trade and moneylending by western banks has generated not only opportunities for profit, but also problems of debtor-creditor relations. Debt servicing difficulties encountered by east European and other borrowers is only one aspect of these problems. Prudent foresight is necessary if we are to avoid an international market and banking breakdown. I hope Canada and its partners will work co-operatively to help resolve this problem without delay. This trade and lending explosion developed in the atmosphere of detente.
External Affairs
For this reason, as well as for others, we must also review the development of this detente especially as it has affected compliance or non-compliance with the commitments undertaken in the Helsinki Final Act. This is what the Belgrade review meeting of the Helsinki Final Act is all about. The major and most popular subject of this meeting is the need to respect human rights. The world-wide trend to assert individual and collective aspirations has produced human rights movements which must not be ignored. This trend carries significant implications for east-west relations, and in particular for NATO-Warsaw Pact relations and relations within the Commonwealth.
Having observed the Canadian delegation working at the Belgrade meeting, I can report to this House that Canada's stand on human rights in particular is being clearly and courageously expounded and upheld. Our team is on the offensive and is bringing to task those signatory countries that have violated their commitments and are suppressing human rights principles enshrined in the Helsinki Final Act and in other human rights covenants and declarations as well as in many modern constitutions, including those of the Soviet Union and the east European countries.
Furthermore, the Helsinki Final Act recognizes the collective rights of peoples to self-determination and equal status in the international community as well as freedom of religious belief and practice. Western advocacy of respect for human rights must be intensified and apply equally to all countries, not just on a selective basis; it must arise from our genuine appreciation of the intrinsic value of each human being and from our conviction that respect for human rights is the best guarantee for peace.
The pursuit of justice in international relations transcends every other obligation. Unfortunately, the Charter of the United Nations has been breached many times. We sadly recall the invasion of our sister Commonwealth country, Cyprus. Last month, both the UN Security Council and the General Assembly spoke in favour of an early and just solution of the Cyprus question. Because the members of the United Nations are obligated by these resolutions, I urge Canada, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), to pursue their implementation vigorously. The people of Cyprus stand on the side of legality and justice. They demand not just sympathy, not just judicial endorsement of their rights, but action.
As in the case of Cyprus and that of many other unfortunate countries where human rights are being violated, we, most fortunate among the countries of the world, are challenged for the sake of justice and peace. In facing this challenge we support the efforts of Canada's representatives under the leadership of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the hope that a rule of justice will bring in true and lasting peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday this debate got under way with a very remarkable speech by the minister, who offered us the hope that this debate could be conducted on a level which would enhance Canada's standing

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
in international affairs. Unfortunately some of the speakers who followed sort of spoiled the possibilities that this debate presented in that regard.
Before 1 turn to the main theme of my remarks I should like to draw the attention of the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) to the fact that the minister did more than mention Spain in his speech. He went to Spain last month on an official visit to that country-the first visit of a Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs to Spain. In my judgment that is more significant than mentioning a country in a speech. I should like, also, to express the regret felt by some of my hon. friends that they did not have an opportunity to take part in this debate.

I particularly wish to mention my colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), the chairman of the committee on external affairs and national defence, who asked me to add his name to the list of speakers. He would have liked also to make his contribution and state some arguments which are worth listening to. 1 also regret that some of my colleagues who were well prepared and ready to take part in this debate were unfortunately unable to make their contribution for lack of time.

1 should like to begin by expressing Canada's regard for a most important group of nations, the Commonwealth countries. Canada remains strongly attached to the Commonwealth and confirms the positive role it can play in world affairs. It continues to evolve as a valuable association of equal, sovereign states which have voluntarily agreed to consult and co-operate in a uniquely flexible and pragmatic manner. Combining 36 countries of different races, languages, cultures and states of economic development from all parts of the world, it reflects accurately the world's current major problems and provides a forum in which consultation, co-operation, and consensus have been developed to a high degree. The Commonwealth has played an important role in a wide variety of political, economic, and social problems of international concern, including that of disparity between rich and poor nations.
The Commonwealth heads of government, meeting in London last June, directed their discussion to major world and Commonwealth trends. A major topic was the situation in southern Africa. They reaffirmed their full support for the struggle in Zimbabwe and Namibia and for the demands of the oppressed in South Africa. They recognized the need to increase the reasons available to broaden Commonwealth programs of humanitarian and technical assistance in that area.
Another major topic was the world economic situation in the light of the results of the North-South Conference and the London Economic Summit. Discussion included the final report of the Commonwealth Group of Experts, which has made a significant contribution to international efforts to evolve a new economic order with particular emphasis on the problems of developing countries. Heads of government

indicated that the Commonwealth has a useful role to play in achieving a global consensus in economic affairs, and considered how it could assist in specific problems such as commodities, energy, food production, trade and finance.
Other topics discussed included the Middle East, Cyprus, the Law of the Sea, human rights, and a review of the large number of functional areas in which Commonwealth co-operation is carried on through the Commonwealth Secretariat and related institutions.
Believing as it does in the ideals and the consensus approach of the Commonwealth, Canada plays an active role in its major ongoing economic and social programs. These are largely co-ordinated through the Commonwealth Secretariat in London and designed particularly to assist developing countries. The Commonwealth Secretary-General said that the Commonwealth has one fourth of the world's people, but it has nearly one half of the world's poor. This adds to Canada's responsibilities.
In pursuing its Commonwealth role, Canada also reinforces its commitment to the broader world community and the ideals of the United Nations. It is also of interest and gratification to Canada that the Commonwealth now includes two other members that also participate in La Francophonie, namely, the governments of Mauritius and the Seychelles.
I should like to turn to the question of disarmament. The hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) asked what initiatives Canada will be taking at the United Nations special session on disarmament. Also they asked what arrangements were being made for participation by members of parliament and other interested Canadians at the session. The definitive Canadian position for the special session remains to be developed in the next few months, and it is the subject of intensive study. However, even at this preparatory stage Canada has already submitted a number of action-oriented proposals relating to the special session. These have included the establishment, under the auspices of the United Nations Secretary General, of an international register of arms transfers to which all member states of the United Nations should submit full information; a conference between both recipients and suppliers to restrain such transfers on a regional basis; regional arms control conferences to deal with local arms races through agreed measures of restraint; and the holding of a follow-up special session at an unspecified interval to review progress in the specific targets to be set by this special session.
It is not expected that the delegation to the special session will be chosen until a month or so before the session begins. In the meantime contacts and consultations are under way with Canadian experts, non-governmental organizations and private individuals concerned about disarmament questions.
The hon. member for Greenwood expressed some apprehension as to the development and the production of the neutron bomb. Perhaps I should indicate that Canada has spoken out in regard to the neutron bomb. The government was asked what position Canada was taking in NATO on the neutron bomb. While Canada has no plans to acquire such weapons,
December 20, 1977

we have been participating in discussions at NATO headquarters in Brussels regarding the possible acquisition by certain NATO countries of enhanced radiation reduced-blast nuclear weapons. These discussions are continuing. The military usefulness of the weapon is not in question but, like our allies, Canada is also conscious that its possible acquisition raises very complex questions which must be examined with utmost care. Any decision regarding these weapons will not be taken lightly.
I believe the hon. Leader of the Opposition, as well as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), raised questions concerning the maritime boundaries negotiations. In their remarks they stated that the Canadian public has not been made aware of the scope of the maritime boundaries negotiations, and that Canadian fishermen, as the most vitally interested constituency, have been denied input with respect to the bilateral negotiations.
The Department of External Affairs, in a press release on October 21, 1977, published the entire text of the Joint Report by Chief Negotiators on Canada/United States Maritime Boundaries and Related Resource Issues, signed by Ambassadors Marcel Cadieux of Canada and Lloyd N. Cutler of the United States, together with annexes on the principles for a joint fisheries commission to be established by a convention between Canada and the United States, and the proposed principles for offshore hydrocarbon shared-access zones.
A subsequent departmental release of November 28 announced the extension of the negotiators' mandates to January 31, 1978, noting that the extra period would permit careful review of the elements involved in the negotiations, for example, management and sharing of fish stocks off both coasts, hydrocarbon sharing arrangements in maritime boundary areas and delimitation of maritime boundaries. The release went on to say that additional time is also required to ensure consultation with and participation by industry, state, provincial, congressional and other interests of the two countries.
From the start the Canadian negotiating team has made every effort to ensure that the fishing industry has been fully and regularly consulted at every stage of the negotiations. Most recently at an east coast fisheries meeting in Boston, from November 28 to December 2, and at a west coast meeting in Vancouver from December 6 to 8, Ambassador Cadieux and his officials held lengthy and extensive consultations with representatives of a wide variety of industry interests. I have a list of 32 interested industries that have been invited to attend those negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, I might give some more information about the involvement of the Canadian government as regards Frenchspeaking countries. I wish to add to what the minister said on another aspect of our foreign policy, the French-speaking countries and the fifth general assembly of its main institution, the Agency for Cultural and Technical Co-operation which has just taken place in Abidjan, Ivory Coast.
The French-speaking countries are an essential element of our international relations because, Mr. Speaker, they are the
External Affairs
natural outside extension of French Canada's vitality and culture. It is also a very useful area of international co-operation. That is why the Canadian government has played a paramount part in the establishment and development of the agency and of ministerial conferences in the areas of education, youth and sports. This is why as well we have facilitated the development of the agency and its programs of training and cultural, educational and technical exchanges, as well as their extension to the scientific field and economic co-operation, two very important areas for the young developing French-speaking countries
From the very beginning, Quebec, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba have contributed to the work of the agency through federal government participation. It was with our help that as early as 1971 Quebec obtained the status of a participating government, and was able to participate very actively in the works of the agency, in co-operation with the federal government. We had given our support to the granting of such status, precisely for governments of federal countries like ours and we consider that such arrangements give evidence of the capabilities of the federal system.
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the parliamentary secretary but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that speaking at this time in the debate before we adjourn for the Christmas recess in my chosen profession it would be more appropriate it I were to announce the benediction rather than offer any remarks with respect to the issue that is before us in terms of the motion.
I doubt whether in my time as a member of parliament I have ever debated a motion which offered as much possibility to literally cover the world horizon as has this particular motion. In the course of the two day debate we have covered enough different opinions and enough of the areas of international conflict and contact to realize that, as the minister himself said in his closing remarks, in the words of Dickens I think, "It was the best of times and it was the worst of times." In some ways that is partially a description of this debate.
We have heard some encouraging words and some discouraging words. In fact I think in almost every speech that was delivered in the House in the past two days we have received both encouragement and discouragement. That was evident in the tempo and mood of the debate in the opening day, in first, the comments of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), who is not here, inadvertently, I suspect, in his answer to the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom) with respect to the Export Development Corporation. It was evident also in the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) who, interestingly enough, stepped from the portfolio of industry, trade and commerce into external affairs.

December 20, 1977
External Affairs
Encapsuled in their remarks, and as picked up by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) today, we have the essential conflict that is at the root of so much of the difficulties we face as a country and as the world. It is the conflict of the question of crass politics or economic interests as against the higher levels of mankind with respect to questions of morality and altruism. None of us can claim to be disinterested in either aspect of that debate. Certainly when the Secretary of State for External Affairs introduced the new initiatives that were to be taken with respect to South Africa which he described as the most clear cut case of specific institutionalized discrimination, many members on all sides could agree. In the context of what has happened at the United Nations since its establishment in 1945 there has come to be a unanimity of opinion with respect to the total abhorrence for institutionalized racial discrimination.
However, what is not so clear, and what came out in the course of questioning earlier today and in some comments over the past two days, is that increasingly we are called upon to make moral decisions with respect to economic and political activity. This should not be surprising to anybody in the House if we look at the major conferences at which the United Nations has focused its attention over the past five to ten years on questions of environment, population, food and habitation, and the last two special sessions on developing a new international economic order. It is fair to say that in each of these instances we were dealing with technological problems, historical problems, and problems related to our own ability to cope with developments in the world community. But I think in the final analysis, when we look at any one of these problems, we realize that whether we would make progress with respect to them really depended on political will.
Recently in speaking to another group I was tempted to suggest that in all the ages of mankind which we have been experiencing in the past few centuries, from the age of steam and the age of steel to the nuclear age, perhaps future historians will look at the period of the late 1960s and 1970s and describe these times not so much as the age of technology or computerization, or as the nuclear age, but rather as the age of morality.
Certainly if we look at the most powerful country in the world led by the new Carter administration, the leading edge of their activity in the international field has to do with accepting some form of moral responsibility. In a way this is what the minister touched upon in his speech, and to the degree that it is a moral responsibility, which we take without hypocrisy and in a genuine attempt to let the world know, and specifically let the authorities in South Africa know, that the system of apartheid is no longer acceptable in the world community, we support him in that initiative. To the degree, however, that it may not, or in some way may touch upon more difficulties for those who are presently suffering from discrimination and from the kind of deliberate or accidental economic and social disparity which exists in these countries, we will need to be more convinced that our approach will be consistent and, in the final analysis, just.
[Mr. MacDonald (Egmont).l
I,	as one individual, welcome the opportunity to debate the matters that have been brought before us today. If I had more time in this debate I would have wanted to talk about the importance of the upcoming UN session on disarmament. Quite frankly I had hoped that the minister, in his quite long address yesterday, might have touched in more detail on what our position was going to be with respect to that assembly. In the time I spent at the United Nations this fall it was not easy to discover whether or not we would either be joining other initiatives with like minded countries or whether we would be taking some initiatives ourselves with regard to this important special assembly next May and June.
I had hoped we could have paid more attention to what is now a new perception on the world food question. Since the World Food Conference met three years ago there have been a number of major changes regarding our understanding on how we are going to solve world food needs, and when we talk about human rights there is no more important and basic human right than the right to a daily nutritious diet.
These are matters that cannot be dealt with in the context of a two-day debate, but I hope the final remarks of the Leader of the Opposition urging a consistent and continuing reference to the major committee which has served this House, namely, the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, will be taken seriously by the minister and by other members of the cabinet.
If Canada is to play an increasingly responsible and constructive role in the world community it will not be seen to be just a matter of debate once every 17 years of a general nature as we have had in the last two days, but the government will accept, with the support of all members in the House, a continuous and perhaps a deepened responsibility in the realm of that committee. A number of members of the committee- the former chairman has just spoken-in the experience they have given to that committee have shown that it can play a responsible role for this parliament and for the Canadian people. If that suggestion alone is acted upon, this debate will have achieved a good deal in terms of Canada's responsible performance in the world community.

subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM TO CONSERVE NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY
ENERGY-POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM TO CONSERVE NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 last. I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) whether the government intended to implement a program urging Canadians to use renewable energy resources such as solar energy, wind energy, geothermal energy and a host of other sources of renewable energy.
Up until recently, people in Canada and elsewhere were taking for granted that the available amounts of energy, those most readily available in the form of wood fossils, coal, were inexhaustible. After the advent of offshore oil, energy was so cheap that we could disregard insulating our oil-heated homes, build big cars without worrying about fuel consumption, manufacture cheap electricity in power hungry oil-fired ther-

December 20, 1977
Adjournment Debate
mal generators. Oil then became the wealth running the world. Because of the escalation of black gold prices of limited supplies, of the economic impact on several countries, we now have to reconsider our position particularly with regard to our oil reserves which we all know now are not inexhaustible. Based on the best predictions, oil production will not be able to meet demand by the year 2,000, and shortages could start between 1985 and 1995.
As far as energy conservation is concerned, we have no alternative. On the other hand, to obtain new sources of energy, we must choose among the possible options those which suit our needs better without going deep into debt or destroying our environment. So, in addition to conservation, we will have to seek a solution through research and development of our renewable energy resources.
In answer to my question as to whether the government intended to implement a national incentive program for conservation, research and development, the minister stated the federal government had decided to significantly increase its expenditures in that area. The government now has a $128.2 million budget for energy research and development. Indeed, the increase proposed for 1978-79 is $15 million. I am also informed that the increase will be from $7.7 million to $15.7 million for research and development of renewable energy sources, which is not bad, and there will also be a $5 million increase to $16.7 million for research and development in energy conservation.
Therefore, it is encouraging to note that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources puts an emphasis on renewable energy sources by doubling next year's estimates, and that he stresses energy conservation measures. The announcement made this week by the minister that his department will propose a $21.9 million funding for the federal labour-intensive program to create jobs and help Canadians save is also a forward step.
Access to information, Mr. Speaker, means perhaps helping Canadians to better insulate their homes and better estimate the performance of their oil or gas heating facilities. It is also perhaps helping Canadians in information and energy conservation oriented projects undertaken at the local level. All of that will contribute to a better utilization of our energy resources. These programs will certainly be useful if we want to explain the urgent nature of the situation and make people understand the kind of challenge that has to be met. Perhaps we might also have to switch some day to incentive programs such as subsidies, grants, tax relief if we want to encourage Canadians to invest and perhaps change their traditional use of what is commonly referred to as energy forms such as oil, coal and gas.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I received a letter from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources informing me that he intends to create in my riding a community centre for energy conservation. This community centre will employ some seven people and its objective will be essentially to inform the public, to give
[Mr. Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier).l
assistance to volunteer agencies, schools, industries, municipalities and citizens' committees to plan and implement energy conservation programs. I can only command the minister for the emphasis he puts on the use of renewable energy resources. I hope that some day we might be able to engage in national programs that the Canadian people may be required to implement, and I leave it to the parliamentary secretary to tell us whether we have or may expect such a national incentive program for the conservation of these renewable energies.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Gilles Lamontagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM TO CONSERVE NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), I must confirm at the outset that one of the main objectives of the national energy policy regarding self-sufficiency is to find possible energy sources which would replace those now being used. The use of solar energy to heat water in private homes and in industries as well as to heat buildings could considerably improve our national energy budget in the long run.
Building insulation is a well established technique used in a modern market and well suited to classic consumer incentives. However, solar heating is only at the exploratory stage. It will soon become economical but it is not yet suited to the above-mentioned classic incentives.
Some other issues must be resolved before the development of an incentive program. It includes the formulation of technical standards for solar heating systems, consumer protection, judicial rights concerning solar rays, zoning and other problems under provincial jurisdiction. The renewable energy resources branch recently created within the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources actively studies those matters in co-operation with other government organizations, at federal and provincial level.
In the solar energy field, the federal government directs its efforts towards research, development and demonstration of the technical feasibility of solar heating in Canada. Spendings in that area have rapidly increased from $100,000 in 1975-76 to more than $4 million for this fiscal year. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced during the debate on the Speech from the Throne that the quasi totality of the supplementary amount of $15 million that must be spent for research and development in the energy field will be directed towards renewable resources and energy conservation. The technical developments of solar heating in Canada take advantage of those research and development efforts. The production and distribution of solar heating equipment will require federal government support as the industry will expand and develop. If such traditional consumer incentives as the Canadian Home Insulation Program are not adequate now, they could become so later on following the research that has been undertaken. So we are very optimistic as concerns the future development of solar heating and other resources of that kind.
December 20, 1977

subtopic: INDUSTRY-NICKEL-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PREVENT LAY-OFFS
INDUSTRY-NICKEL-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PREVENT LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a most disheartening sight to see members get ready to leave here in order to have a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. As the members exchanged greetings, I thought of the 5,000 to 6,000 unemployed or about to be unemployed workers in the Sudbury basin who will not be able to contemplate dumplings and sugar plums over this Christmas season. With that in mind, I was prompted to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today what specific measures the government has and is prepared to announce in the New Year with regard to the nickel industry in order to avoid the lay-offs that will occur there at the end of January or the beginning of February.
Already the workers are receiving notices. It is now extending to the salaried workers. Workers with 21 years' experience at INCO have received their notice-48 years old with 21 years' service with the company. Workers today started receiving notices informing them that they are now being downgraded in terms of the jobs they are doing. If you are a machinist, you are now a labourer. Of course it involves a pay cut. All of this is taking place in the Sudbury basin. It has created a very unsound economic picture there.
I felt it was my responsibility to place these questions before the Prime Minister today. I asked what steps he is contemplating to put before the House when it returns in January with regard to the unemployment situation in the nickel industry. The Prime Minister stated it would take some time before they could get around to that. He says it takes time to plan a strategy. This is not new. We have been living with a hinterland economy for a long time.
A majority Liberal government has been in power for the greater part of the last 50 years. We have lived in Ontario with a provincial Conservative government for the last 40 years. Therefore they cannot hide behind any excuse that they have been unable to plan. But they have failed to plan and thus have developed one industry communities such as we have in the Sudbury basin.
I asked the Prime Minister to consider the pattern that has been set by the French and the United States in stockpiling nickel. That was not an idle suggestion of mine; I have suggested it for a long time. I used the example of the government's approach to uranium when in the 1950's and 1960's the industry was faced with the disaster of the community of Elliot Lake being on the verge of collapse.
Let me quote from the 1973 report "An Energy Policy for Canada". This report gives the concise rationale for stockpiling uranium. I quote:
Following the completion of the second uranium stockpiling program in 1970, the federal government announced that, in view of the continuing poor shortterm marketing situation it would consider further assistance for established
Adjournment Debate
uranium mining communities. Subsequently, the federal government entered into an agreement with Denison to jointly stockpile-
What the government did was to stockpile uranium for seven years. The rationale for this was that it was not just a strategic mineral. The fact is that the government was concerned about the economy of that community. We are now suggesting to the government that the same rationale should be used to stockpile nickel today.
Who caused the lay-offs at INCO? Surely it was not the workers. Who was it that made the decision 30 months ago to continue to stockpile nickel? Who was it made the decision to continue demanding overtime for production workers? Surely it is not the workers who participate in such decision making. No, Mr. Speaker, it was INCO and Falconbridge, in full knowledge of the situation. They have always kept that information close to their breast and have never shared it with the government, as we know from the record, or with the workers. It was the company which made a unilateral decision to continue to stockpile nickel.
The Prime Minister said that the companies are carrying a seven month supply. According to INCO's 1976 annual report, the company's nickel inventories at year end were equivalent to a five to six months' supply as compared with a normal level of two to three months' supply. We know that a the end of 1976 the company was carrying six months' stockpile. We are now told they are carrying a seven months' supply. In other words, over the period of one year they have maintained their stockpile. It is rather interesting that from the end of 1976 to the end of 1977 they have maintained a seven months' stockpile when they normally carry two or three months' supply.
The question has to be asked; if the company is prepared to carry that kind of stockpile, surely it is well aware that the turnaround of the nickel market is just around the corner? All of the experts in the nickel industry have told us so. We have been through the copper downturn and copper is now taking off. The American government is about to announce the stockpiling of copper. Therefore we have told the government that it has a responsibility to the workers in the Sudbury basin. It cannot leave the workers to the vicissitudes of the unilateral decision by the company to plan its production level; the government is culpably responsible for the conditions of the nickel mining industry in the Sudbury basin. Only they can lift the sword of Damocles from the heads of the workers in the Sudbury basin-

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Gilles Lamontagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
subtopic: INDUSTRY-NICKEL-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PREVENT LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member's question on the possible stockpiling of nickel, may I say that the parallel with the uranium stockpiling program is fairly distant. In the case of uranium we were faced with the reality of total mine closures and the economic collapse of the community of Elliot Lake, whereas in the present nickel surplus situation we are facing grave prob-

December 20, 1977
Adjournment Debate
lems of cutbacks in production and employment but not total closures.
Let me repeat what the hon. member already knows. There is a world surplus of nickel production capacity in relation to demand. For going on to three years now, world nickel production has exceeded demand and, as a result, producers around the world have been accumulating inventories which are now at a level far in excess of what has been considered normal. Besides being an onerous burden for the companies, these large inventories have also had an effect in the market place. No easy solution is foreseen for the world-wide problem of oversupply and declining prices. Producers in other countries are facing the same problem as Canadian producers and many of them have announced cutbacks in production similar to those taking place in Canada.
The financing of additional excess nickel inventories directly or indirectly by the federal government would extend the period of excess nickel supply and would involve large financial commitment. It could also be an open invitation for similar programs for other metals which are now in over-supply, and these are many. However, serious as these disadvantages are, the government continues to study urgently all potential solutions and does not rule out any possibility of a workable scheme including those which may involve stockpiling elements.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) mentioned this afternoon the stockpiling program in France. Mr. Speaker, France is an importing country, and when it does stockpile it is to protect herself against a fluctuation in price. When a Canadian company stockpiles it is because it is confronted with a very soft world market and, as I mentioned earlier, stockpiling is a very expensive process. There is a world of difference between the two reasons for stockpiling.
Mr. Speaker, considering that this is the last intervention in the House of Commons in the year 1977, with your permission I should like to extend good wishes to Your Honour and all members of the House in a language which I do not think has been used so far in this connection, though I have heard hon. members on both sides extend their seasonal wishes in English. I should like to say it in French.
[ Translation]
I wish everyone a Merry Christmas and I even wish for the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) that the year 1978 will be a very happy one for all men of goodwill, and we certainly need that.
